name: MXNet
baseline: TensorFlow and PyTorch (TensorFlow 2.3 and PyTorch 1.6.0 from framework examples; NGC TensorFlow 1.15.2 and NGC PyTorch 1.5.0a0 containers)
workload: OneFlow DLPerf report v1.0 (Oct 2020): ResNet-50 v1.5 training throughput in images/s, FP32 batch size 128 per GPU, 1 to 32 Tesla V100 GPUs; also BERT-base pretraining sentences/s.
claimed_speedup: ResNet-50 v1.5 FP32 bsz 128, 1 GPU: MXNet 1.6.0 with gluon-cv 384.19 img/s vs PyTorch 348.62 and TensorFlow 2.x 321.80 (1.10x and 1.19x, derived from page data); NVIDIA NGC MXNet 392.24 vs NGC PyTorch 367.29 and NGC TensorFlow 1.x 362.44. 32 GPUs: NGC MXNet 11331.93 vs NGC PyTorch 10917.09 (1.04x) and NGC TensorFlow 1.x 9514.64 (1.19x), derived from page data. BERT-base FP32 on 32 GPUs: MXNet (W/O clip) 4340.89 sentences/s vs NGC TensorFlow 1.x 3089.74, NGC PyTorch 3039.3, TensorFlow 2.x 2244.38.
compiler_and_flags: Prebuilt framework builds, no compile flags stated: NGC 20.03 containers (nvcr.io/nvidia/mxnet:20.03-py3 with MXNet 1.6.0, DALI and Horovod; tensorflow:20.03-tf1-py3 with 1.15.2; pytorch:20.03-py3 with 1.5.0a0), CUDA 10.2 and driver 440.33.01; upstream rows use MXNet 1.6.0 with gluon-cv, TensorFlow 2.3.0 and PyTorch 1.6.0 examples.
hardware: 4 nodes, each 8x Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB, Intel Xeon Gold 5118 @ 2.30GHz, 384 GB RAM, InfiniBand 100 Gb/s, Ubuntu 16.04.4
tradeoffs: Archived on GitHub 2023-11-17 (read-only); bindings for Python, R, Julia, Scala, Go, JavaScript and more; hybridization between imperative and symbolic execution. Benefits shown depend on NVIDIA's tuned NGC container (DALI, Horovod).
caveats: The benchmark is run by OneFlow, a competing framework, from public scripts in Oneflow-Inc/DLPerf; OneFlow beats MXNet in every row quoted. The MXNet margin is small and not consistent: upstream MXNet 1.6.0 gluon-cv is slower than PyTorch 1.6.0 on 8 GPUs (2556.03 vs 2632.93 img/s) and on 32 GPUs (9579.74 vs 10021.29), and beats TensorFlow 2.3 by only 1.02x there (9418.44). The big NGC MXNet figure comes from NVIDIA's tuned container. The BERT row is 'W/O clip_by_global_norm', which the report says raises throughput and may lower accuracy. The repo README summary shows NGC MXNet 32-GPU FP32 as 11233.92 while the report and sub-README show 11331.93, and AMP 32-GPU as 30713.68 vs 27558.28 in the sub-README. Versions are from 2020, so TensorFlow 2.x and PyTorch 2.x numbers have moved since. An older NeurIPS 2019 PyTorch paper table (MXNet 218, PyTorch 212, TensorFlow 200 img/s, seen only as a search snippet; arXiv and NeurIPS blocked) points the same way. Last commit shown for master is 2023-01-26; the repo is archived.
found_via: seed-record pass; awesome-cpp Artificial Intelligence list entry MXNet, then github.com/apache/mxnet and WebSearch 'MXNet vs TensorFlow vs PyTorch benchmark throughput images/sec ResNet-50 GPU deep-learning-benchmark', which surfaced Oneflow-Inc/DLPerf.

name: PyTorch
baseline: TensorFlow
workload: u39kun/deep-learning-benchmark: forward-pass (eval) and forward+backward (train) time per batch for VGG16, ResNet152 and DenseNet161, 224x224x3 images, batch size 16, FP32 and FP16, on several NVIDIA GPUs using NGC containers.
claimed_speedup: Titan V FP32, PyTorch 0.3.0 vs TensorFlow 1.4.0: vgg16 train 108.8 ms vs 157.2 ms (1.44x), resnet152 train 180.2 ms vs 269.8 ms (1.50x). RTX 2080 Ti FP32, PyTorch 1.0.0 vs TensorFlow 1.12.0: resnet152 train 142.5 ms vs 191.0 ms (1.34x), resnet152 eval 41.8 ms vs 43.6 ms; ratios derived from page data. TensorFlow 1.12.0 is faster on vgg16 train (90.8 ms vs 95.5 ms).
compiler_and_flags: Prebuilt NGC docker images, no build flags: nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:17.12 (0.3.0) and :19.01-py3 (1.0.0), nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorflow:17.12 (1.4.0) and :19.01-py3 (1.12.0); CUDA 9.0.176, cuDNN 7.0.0.5, driver 387.34, or CUDA 10.0.130 with cuDNN 7.4.2.24 for the 2080 Ti rows.
hardware: NVIDIA Titan V, GTX 1080 Ti, Tesla V100 (AWS p3) and RTX 2080 Ti; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Eager-mode Python front end over a C++/CUDA core (ATen, autograd); needs GPU memory and a CUDA or ROCm stack for the GPU speedups.
caveats: The benchmark is a small community repo (u39kun, 427 stars), not project-authored, with 2017-2019 framework versions (PyTorch 0.3.0 and 1.0.0 against TensorFlow 1.4 to 1.12 graph mode), so it says little about TensorFlow 2.x with XLA or PyTorch 2.x. The win is mixed: TensorFlow 1.12 is faster on vgg16 training on the 2080 Ti (90.8 vs 95.5 ms FP32, 58.6 vs 68.1 ms FP16), and eval times are within about 4%. Titan V FP32 vgg16 eval is 31.3 vs 31.8 ms. Results are batch size 16 only. A second independent source, Oneflow-Inc/DLPerf report v1.0 (Oct 2020, 4x8 V100 GPUs, ResNet-50 v1.5 FP32, bsz 128), has PyTorch 1.6.0 10021.29 img/s vs TensorFlow 2.3 9418.44 (1.06x, derived) and NGC PyTorch 10917.09 vs NGC TensorFlow 1.x 9514.64, but with AMP NGC PyTorch 22551.16 loses to NGC TensorFlow with XLA 29171.69; that report was read at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Oneflow-Inc/DLPerf/HEAD/reports/dlperf_benchmark_test_report_v1.md. The PyTorch NeurIPS 2019 paper table (MXNet 218, PyTorch 212, TensorFlow 200 img/s ResNet-50, seen only as a search snippet) was not readable because arXiv and NeurIPS are blocked.

name: Flashlight
baseline: PyTorch 1.8 and TensorFlow 2.4
workload: Wall-clock seconds for 100 iterations of forward plus backward passes including data loading, on six large networks (AlexNet, VGG16, ResNet-50, a BERT-like transformer, an ASR transformer, ViT), on 1 GPU and 8 GPUs with data-parallel gradient synchronization.
claimed_speedup: ICML 2022 paper Table 3 (seconds per 100 iterations, lower is better; order PyTorch / TensorFlow / Flashlight; 1 GPU then 8 GPUs): AlexNet 2.0 / 4.0 / 1.4 then 6.0 / 6.5 / 2.1; VGG16 14.8 / 12.6 / 13.2 then 16.3 / 17.9 / 14.9; ResNet-50 11.1 / 12.4 / 10.3 then 12.3 / 15.9 / 11.9; BERT-like 19.6 / 19.8 / 17.5 then 22.7 / 23.6 / 19.2; ASR transformer 58.5 / 63.7 / 53.6 then 63.7 / 69.7 / 57.5; ViT 137.8 / 140.3 / 129.3 then 143.1 / 169.6 / 141.0. Ratios (derived from page data): AlexNet 1 GPU 1.43x vs PyTorch and 2.86x vs TensorFlow, 8 GPUs 2.86x and 3.10x; ResNet-50 1 GPU 1.08x and 1.20x; ViT 8 GPUs 1.02x vs PyTorch and 1.20x vs TensorFlow. On 1 GPU VGG16 TensorFlow (12.6) beats Flashlight (13.2).
hardware: Intel E5-2698 CPUs with 512 GB RAM, NVIDIA V100-32GB GPUs in a DGX-1 server, NVLink between GPUs for the 8-GPU runs
stars_or_usage: 5.5k stars; Meta (FAIR) project, successor of wav2letter
tradeoffs: Research-oriented C++-only framework (small Python bindings) with a much smaller model and ecosystem than PyTorch or TensorFlow; default tensor backend is ArrayFire with JIT kernel compilation, so it needs ArrayFire plus CUDA, OpenCL or CPU libraries; the fl::Tensor API is marked work in progress with possible API breakage.
caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: arxiv.org, ar5iv, proceedings.mlr.press, icml.cc and ai.meta.com were all EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the paper PDF was never opened; the table and the setup (Flashlight 0.3.1, PyTorch 1.8, TensorFlow 2.4, hardware above) come from WebSearch result excerpts of arXiv 2201.12465, and two separately worded searches returned identical numbers. Peer-reviewed at ICML 2022 (a tier B candidate once the PDF can be read), but written by the Flashlight authors, so first-party. Compiler, flags, build options, framework configuration and whether the benchmark scripts are public were not seen (the README of flashlight/fl/tensor only mentions benchmarks with Flashlight, no benchmark directory was found under flashlight/fl). The gains are under 10 percent on most rows (VGG16, ResNet-50 1 GPU, BERT-like, ASR, ViT), TensorFlow wins VGG16 on 1 GPU, and the large ratios come from AlexNet, a small, overhead-bound model. Framework versions date from 2021. Times include data loading, so they are not pure kernel speed. The awesome-cpp lead lists the license as BSD; GitHub shows MIT.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp#Artificial Intelligence (listing 'fast, flexible machine learning library'); repo page https://github.com/flashlight/flashlight; WebSearch for the ICML 2022 Flashlight paper benchmark table

name: oneDNN
baseline: TensorFlow default CPU kernels (Eigen-based ops)
workload: TensorFlow models run with oneDNN custom ops turned on versus the default Eigen-based TensorFlow CPU ops, as summarised in the TensorFlow RFC that made oneDNN ops default on x86 Linux.
claimed_speedup: Enabling custom oneDNN ops achieves throughput speedups up to 3x in inference and 2.4x in training on a Cascade Lake CPU; additional 1.7-1.9x with bfloat16 on a Cooper Lake CPU; 3-4x on top of software quantization with int8 on a Cascade Lake CPU (RFC text quoting Intel and TensorFlow blog posts).
hardware: Intel Cascade Lake and Cooper Lake Xeon CPUs; exact models not stated in the RFC
stars_or_usage: 4.1k stars; used by PyTorch, TensorFlow, OpenVINO and ONNX Runtime
tradeoffs: Runtime JIT and dynamic dispatch pick AVX-512, AMX, bf16 and int8 kernels per CPU; supports x64, AArch64 (with Arm Compute Library) and Intel GPUs. Results differ slightly in floating-point round-off from default kernels, and the RFC says oneDNN ops can be slower in rare cases from primitive-creation overhead. The README recommends the Intel C++ compiler for best performance on Intel CPUs.
caveats: First-party vendor claim: the RFC is by Intel and TensorFlow engineers and its numbers come from Intel Medium and blog posts that were blocked here, so only the RFC's summary was read; model list, batch sizes, TensorFlow version and flags are not given on the page. 'Up to' figures are best cases. TensorFlow has since turned oneDNN ops on by default in x86 Linux builds, so the baseline of default Eigen ops no longer exists unless disabled with TF_ENABLE_ONEDNN_OPTS=0. No head-to-head against OpenBLAS or MKL was found: the issue #415 search hit has no numbers. The project is now governed by the UXL Foundation and is also reachable at github.com/uxlfoundation/oneDNN.
found_via: seed-record pass; awesome-cpp Artificial Intelligence list entry oneDNN, then github.com/oneapi-src/oneDNN and the tensorflow/community RFC 20210930-enable-onednn-ops found via WebSearch 'oneDNN speedup TensorFlow with oneDNN enabled vs default Eigen up to 3x CPU inference benchmark ResNet-50 images/sec'.

name: evm.zig (evmz, Zig EVM execution engine)
baseline: evmone (v0.23.0, baseline and advanced interpreters) and revm (=43.0.2 raw interpreter, Interpreter::run_plain)
workload: VM-core 'compare' lane over the evm-bench-style fixtures (arithmetic loop, MSTORE loop, keccak loop, ten-thousand-hashes, SLOAD and SSTORE loops, LOG0/LOG4 with 0 and 32 byte data, ERC20 mint, transfer and approval+transfer, snailtracer): deployed runtime bytecode called repeatedly through each engine's interpreter-level path with analysis prepared outside the timed window, fixed Osaka spec, median of 100-run medians, lower time is better.
claimed_speedup: README (Apple M1 Max, ReleaseFast, 2026-08-13), evmz versus evmone-base versus revm-int: Arithmetic loop 0.104 / 0.109 / 0.501 ms, Storage SSTORE loop 0.162 / 0.854 / 0.875 ms, ERC20 transfer 3.761 / 6.247 / 6.084 ms, Snailtracer 19.965 / 59.804 / 37.990 ms. bench/README.md ratios (base/evmz and revm/evmz): SSTORE 5.27x and 5.40x, SLOAD 3.97x and 2.34x, snailtracer 3.00x and 1.90x, ERC20 transfer 1.66x and 1.62x, Arithmetic 1.05x and 4.82x. evmz is slower than evmone-base on MSTORE loop (0.125 vs 0.084 ms, 0.67x), LOG0 32-byte (0.057 vs 0.033 ms, 0.58x), LOG0 0-byte (0.69x), LOG4 0-byte (0.80x) and ten-thousand-hashes (0.86x). AMD EPYC Genoa (KVM guest pinned to one CPU) rows are near parity with evmone-base: ERC20 transfer 7.686 vs 7.447 ms (0.97x), arithmetic 0.151 vs 0.145 ms (0.96x), keccak loop 4.597 vs 4.584 ms (1.00x), snailtracer 33.347 vs 57.983 ms (1.74x), SSTORE 0.595 vs 0.838 ms (1.41x), and ahead of revm on every row (1.08x to 3.08x).
compiler_and_flags: Zig >= 0.16.0, zig build bench-compare -Dbench-optimize=ReleaseFast -Dbench-support-min=osaka -Dbench-support-max=osaka -Dnative-keccak=xkcp -- --spec osaka --num-runs 100 --warmup-ms 100 (five repeats, median); all engines built without frame pointers (evmone via -fomit-frame-pointer inside the Zig build, evmone v0.23.0 with intx 0.15.0); revm 43.0.2 built with Cargo --release, RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=native -C force-frame-pointers=no, fat LTO, one codegen unit.
hardware: Apple M1 Max, macOS arm64 (headline snapshot, 2026-08-13); AMD EPYC Genoa, Linux x86-64, KVM guest pinned to one CPU (earlier snapshot).
tradeoffs: Tail-call-dispatch interpreter in Zig with fork rules, tracing and single-step selected at compile time (separate binaries), zero-alloc pooled executor, optional XKCP Keccak and native crypto libraries (blst, mcl, libsecp256k1) as lazy dependencies, zkVM guest builds (ZisK, SP1, OpenVM). The headline numbers enable the optional XKCP Keccak provider ('maximum-performance configuration'). Pre-1.0 (version 0.0.0), builds need a very recent Zig (0.16).
caveats: Comparison is VM-core only: interpreter execute() with analysis prepared outside the timed window, no transaction validation, journal or database, so it is not a whole-client comparison (the repo says the executor lane is deliberately later). Correctness check in all three runners is limited to a success status (evmz result.status() == success, evmone EVMC_SUCCESS, revm result.is_ok()); the compare lane does not assert that return data, gas used or log counts match across engines (it only records host call counts). The README headline table shows the four rows where evmz wins; the full M1 table also has rows where evmone-baseline is faster (MSTORE loop, LOG0 and LOG4 rows, ten-thousand-hashes), and on the AMD snapshot evmz is within about 7% of evmone-base on 9 of 14 rows (ratios 0.94x to 1.07x, derived from page data) and slower on the LOG0 rows (0.73x, 0.75x). The AMD snapshot is older and run in a KVM guest. Revm is timed through its raw interpreter, not a transaction path. The repo contains CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md (AI-assisted development); first-party numbers only, 3 stars. Not the cryptuon/zig-evm project, which is rejected for a hard-coded table.

compiler_and_flags: Baselines built as: node run-v8.mjs <case>.js for V8; asc <case>.as.ts -O3 for AssemblyScript; native references clang -O3 -march=native, rustc -C opt-level=3 -C target-cpu=native; jz compile(src, { optimize: 'speed' }); clang 19.1.6, jz 0.9.2, asc 0.28.19 (results.json meta).
hardware: Apple M4 Max (darwin/arm64)
name: jz (dy/jz)
baseline: V8 (Node.js) running the same JavaScript, plus AssemblyScript
workload: Numeric JavaScript kernels (DSP, audio, image, hashing, parsing, simulation; 63 cases, 55 with parity against V8) compiled ahead of time to WebAssembly by jz and run on Node's V8 Wasm engine, versus the same source as raw JS on Node/V8.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Faster than V8 and AssemblyScript on almost every kernel we measure, about 2x on average'. Committed bench/results.json (Apple M4 Max, Node v25.9.0): geometric mean of per-case median time ratios jz/V8 0.443 over 55 checksum-verified cases (about 2.26x faster, faster on 52 of 55); jz/AssemblyScript 0.448 over 50 cases (faster on 44); jz in wasmtime 0.498 of V8 (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Compiles a statically analyzable JavaScript subset: no GC (bump allocator), no eval or Proxy, fixed object shapes, regexes at build time, 32-bit array indices, 64-bit wrapping BigInt. Pre-1.0.
caveats: Compares compiled-to-Wasm code against V8 running the same JS on numeric kernels chosen by the author, with the project's own harness; ratios here are this agent's geometric means from results.json rows with parity 'ok' (the bench page jz.js.org was not opened). V8 loses mostly because of dynamic-typing overhead the subset removes, not because Wasm is a faster VM. The harness records a per-case verdict and notes rows that are only a tie.

baseline: wazero (WebAssembly runtime for Go; version and execution mode not stated)
workload: pgaskin/go-marisa BenchmarkTrie (a WebAssembly build of the MARISA trie called from Go, Words and Go125 datasets): build, ReadFrom, WriteTo, marshal and unmarshal, lookup, reverse lookup, predictive and common-prefix search; wazero-bound build against wasm2go-transpiled build, benchstat of 6 runs.
claimed_speedup: benchstat sec/op, wasm2go against wazero: geomean 109.5us -> 92.58us (-15.45%); Trie/Go125/Lookup 96.77ns -> 70.31ns (-27.34%); Trie/Words/ReverseLookup 123.65ns -> 73.63ns (-40.45%); Trie/Words/Lookup 344.2ns -> 306.8ns (-10.87%); Trie/Words/WriteTo 11.383us -> 2.541us (-77.68%); CommonPrefixSearchSeq -12% to -18%. Slower: Trie/Words/Build 349.4ms -> 406.9ms (+16.46%), Trie/Go125/Build +34.67%, Trie/Words/UnmarshalBinary 323.6us -> 634.8us (+96.16%). Keys/s geomean 2.525M -> 2.802M (+10.97%).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26 (go1.26.0): CGO_ENABLED=0 go test -v -run='^$' -bench=BenchmarkTrie -count=6 github.com/pgaskin/go-marisa; wasm2go commit 075b64a04783d6c188ac9f66ea52688bc71edb9e; wazero version not stated
hardware: Lenovo T14s Gen 6, Intel(R) Core(TM) Ultra 7 258V (linux/amd64, 8 threads), performance mode
stars_or_usage: 237 stars; adopted by ncruces/go-sqlite3 and pgaskin/go-marisa
tradeoffs: Translates a Wasm module to self-contained Go source with no dependencies beyond Go, so no runtime and no cgo; the output is deliberately unreadable (goto labels, type conversions) and its speed depends on the Go compiler's assembly. A static translation: runtime loading of arbitrary modules still needs wazero (stated in the discussion). Large generated files cost compile time and memory (a commenter in discussion #361 reported about 40 seconds and 4 GB of RAM to compile). Each module instance keeps its own memory up to 4 GB.
caveats: Mixed result on one workload and one machine: queries and WriteTo are faster, build and some read paths are slower, so the geomean win (-15.45%) hides regressions up to +96%. Run by pgaskin (the go-marisa author) rather than the wasm2go author, which makes it independent, but the wazero version and the flags used to build the MARISA Wasm blob are not stated; go-marisa's README summarises the same switch as 'slightly faster at querying, but about 50% slower at building/reading/writing'. Not the go-sqlite3 workload that the discussion is about. Separate project from goccy/wasm2go.

name: PolkaVM
baseline: Wasmtime (cranelift); the same table also lists Wasmtime winch, Wasmer singlepass, Wasm3, Wasmi, wazero, CKB VM and Solana RBPF
workload: Three guest programs (pinky, a cycle-accurate NES emulator running a homebrew game; prime-sieve; minimal) built for PolkaVM's RISC-V RV32EM ISA and for WebAssembly for the other VMs; one-shot time including compilation and initialization, steady-state execution time, and compile time.
claimed_speedup: One-shot (compile + init + run) on pinky: PolkaVM 64-bit recompiler 55.408 ms vs Wasmtime (cranelift) 116.002 ms and Wasmer (singlepass) 137.832 ms (about 2.1x and 2.5x, derived from page data); prime-sieve: 14.390 ms vs Wasmtime cranelift 125.107 ms, Wasmtime winch 54.295 ms, Wasmer singlepass 57.379 ms (about 8.7x, 3.8x, 4.0x, derived from page data); compile time on pinky 167.553 us vs Wasmtime cranelift 62.212 ms (about 370x, derived from page data). Steady-state execution is not faster: pinky 6.422 ms vs Wasmtime cranelift 5.776 ms; prime-sieve 2.104 ms vs 2.161 ms (parity).
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.86.0 (rust-toolchain.toml); benchtool built with cargo --release (profile: lto = true, codegen-units = 1); guests built by guest-programs/build-benchmarks.sh (wasm32-unknown-unknown, RISC-V targets); benchtool Cargo.toml at HEAD pins wasmtime 26.0.1, wasmer 5.0.0, wasmi 0.39.1; replication steps (01-build-benchmarks.sh, 02-run-benchmarks.rb, 03-analyze-benchmarks.rb) listed on the page
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3970X 32-Core, x86_64 Linux; results from commit 190ea5ac, timestamp 2024-11-24
tradeoffs: Guests must be compiled for PolkaVM's own RV32EM RISC-V ISA, not WebAssembly; no floating point or SIMD by design; Rust host API (no C API seen in the workspace); sandboxing and gas metering are built in; the interpreter fallback is far slower (pinky 1.689 s one-shot vs 55.408 ms recompiler); README says the project is unfinished and a heavy work in progress.
caveats: Numbers date from November 2024 (Wasmtime 26, Wasmer 5), long before current Wasmtime releases; first-party suite where the workloads were chosen by the PolkaVM author; the VMs execute different binaries (RISC-V for PolkaVM, Wasm for the rest); the win is in one-shot and compile time, while Wasmtime cranelift is faster or equal in steady-state execution on pinky and prime-sieve; the compile-time gap is likely partly because Wasmtime cranelift optimizes while PolkaVM's recompiler is single-pass (README: guaranteed single-pass O(n) compilation).

name: risechain/pevm (parallel EVM on revm)
baseline: sequential revm (pevm's own execute_revm_sequential path)
workload: Criterion (100 samples) wall time to execute one whole Ethereum block with state preloaded in memory: 85 real mainnet blocks from Frontier to Cancun, plus three mocked 1-Gigagas blocks (raw transfers, ERC20 transfers, Uniswap swaps); sequential revm versus pevm's Block-STM style parallel executor.
claimed_speedup: Benches README: Uniswap Swaps gigagas block 413.42 ms sequential vs 18.707 ms parallel (22.1x); ERC20 Transfers 246.43 vs 60.817 ms (4.05x); Raw Transfers 159.08 vs 56.425 ms (2.82x). Mainnet blocks: 'We are currently ~2.02 times faster than sequential execution on average', max speed-up x4.32 (block 7279999, 4.54 ms vs 1.05 ms), max slow-down x0.89. Top-level README repeats '2x faster than sequential execution on average for Ethereum blocks, and 22x faster ... for a Gigagas block of independent Uniswap swaps'. In the 85-row mainnet table (counted from page data), 63 blocks are more than 5% faster, 18 are within 5% of 1.0 and 4 are slower (0.89x to 0.93x).
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --features global-alloc (mainnet bench) and JEMALLOC_SYS_WITH_MALLOC_CONF=thp:always,metadata_thp:always cargo bench --features global-alloc --bench gigagas; workspace Cargo.toml release profile codegen-units=1, lto=fat, panic=abort; global allocator rpmalloc on x86 and snmalloc on aarch64 for mainnet, jemalloc with THP for gigagas; concurrency level 8 on x86 / 12 on ARM; rustc version not pinned (no rust-toolchain file, edition 2024).
hardware: AWS c7g.8xlarge, Graviton3, 32 vCPUs @ 2.6 GHz
tradeoffs: Parallel executor that still delegates VM execution to revm (an inline parallel-aware EVM is only a TODO). Speedup depends on block parallelism; falls back to sequential execution when a block self-destructs then redeploys a contract, and the concurrency level is hard-coded (8 on x86, 12 on ARM) with the README noting it ideally needs auto-tuning. Needs cmake to build snmalloc. Repo warns it is a work in progress and not production ready.
caveats: Baseline is revm run sequentially inside pevm's own harness (force_sequential flag / execute_revm_sequential), not an independent geth or evmone run; no geth evm comparison exists. Chain state is preloaded into memory, which the authors say understates the parallel advantage versus disk-backed state. The 22x figure is a synthetic mocked gigagas block of independent Uniswap swaps with no dependencies (README says it does not represent real-world blocks); real mainnet blocks average about 2.0x with several blocks at 1.0x or slightly slower. The top-level README's 2x/22x numbers describe the legacy Block-STM design; the 'new' architecture (inline EVM, sparse trie, shreds) is listed under TODO. No rustc version is stated, so tier A rests on public bench code, the release profile in Cargo.toml and a named CPU. Parallel Go (Polygon, Sei) being slower than sequential Rust/C++ is asserted in prose with no numbers.

About 1.6x faster than WAMR fast-interp and 2.1x faster than Pulley on the M4 (derived from page data). Page text: 'wasm3 is the fastest interpreter on nearly every case it runs'.

hardware: Apple M4 Max E-cores (MacBook Pro, macOS 27.0); iPhone XS Max A12 Bionic E-cores (iOS 18.7.10)

In the wasmi-benchmarks suite (AMD EPYC 7763, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks-plots/HEAD/data/amd-epyc-7763/lin-scale/geomean-execute.svg) execute geomean relative to the fastest runtime per test is wasm3 16.51x vs Wasmtime Cranelift 1.15x and V8 1.05x. Of the Wasm 3.0 features the benchmark tested it supports only tail calls and extended-const. Maintainer states the project is in a minimal maintenance phase.

Independent libsodium 2021-Q1 run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks/HEAD/2021-Q1/README.md): WAMR fast-interp slower than wasm3 on every test, native about 30x faster than wasm3 and about 46x faster than WAMR; I derived about 1.5x wasm3 over WAMR from the per-test logs.

claimed_speedup: Instantiate 9.1x (1.724 us vs 15.74 us); interruptible loops with WithCloseOnContextDone 9.8x; memory.fill 1.68x geomean (7.1x at 15 bytes); compiled execution 4-18% (geomean about 6%) on memory-heavy kernels with fibonacci 'a wash'; host calls a tie (47.8 ns vs 48.3 ns); cumulative geomean -17.8% time and -22.9% B/op across internal/integration_test/bench vs the wazero fork point; 6.5 MB Rust module vs wazero v1.12.0: 4.9x compiled and 1.7x interpreted on a 5 MB input, of which the README says most of the 4.9x is the cost of WithCloseOnContextDone on wazero and about 1.3x remains with the option off.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26 (Go 1.26.1 on the third-party run), CGO_ENABLED=0; benchstat over interleaved A/B runs with upstream wazero as control; commands: cd benchmarks/vs-wazero && go test -bench .
hardware: Apple M4 (native arm64) for the head-to-head and cumulative numbers; core-pinned Intel i9-12900HK for memory.grow and interruptible-loop numbers; a third-party run on Apple M5 Pro (18-core), macOS 26.5
tradeoffs: Pure Go, no CGO; has a compiled mode and an interpreter mode (the README benchmarks both and the CLI has an -interpreter flag); adds Component Model, WASI 0.2 and the WASI 0.3 async ABI that wazero lacks; the host-call win comes from deleting reflection-based registration (the API broke compatibility with wazero once). Not callable from C++ directly.
caveats: The baseline is wazero, not Wasmtime, Wasmer, WAMR or V8; the README itself discloses that its largest figures (9.8x, 4.9x) come mostly from what WithCloseOnContextDone costs wazero, and that raw code-generator differences are about 6% geomean to about 30% on the large module; host-call and fibonacci results are ties; the README of a fork (xusenlin/wazy) says 'execution on par with wasmtime and faster than wazero' with no wasmtime numbers, and the current samyfodil/wazy README does not repeat the parity claim; the Wasmtime comparison arms need cgo and are not reported.

name: hxcpp (Haxe C++ backend and runtime)
baseline: NekoVM and HashLink (HL/JIT) Haxe targets; also compared with Haxe's JVM/Java and JavaScript (Node) targets
workload: tong's gist 'Haxe benchmarks' running the HashLink repository's other/benchs suite (Startup, Anonymous, BinaryTrees, Fib, FloatArray, IntArray, Mandelbrot, NBodies) compiled from the same Haxe source to each target (js, cpp, cs, hl, java, lua, neko, php, python; hlc and jvm in the 2025 rerun) and timed in seconds, 2018 run plus a September 2025 rerun in a comment.
claimed_speedup: 2018 run (build:runtime seconds, cpp versus hl versus neko): Anonymous 0.38 / 0.29 / 4.57, BinaryTrees 0.08 / 0.76 / 1.68, Fib 0.01 / 0.08 / 0.42, FloatArray 0.01 / 0.04 / 1.94, IntArray 0.03 / 0.07 / 2.95, Mandelbrot 0.13 / 4.28 / 9.65, NBodies 0.04 / 0.13 / 5.91. Gist total runtime: C++ 0.72 s, Java 0.81, JavaScript 0.96, HashLink 5.68, Neko 27.16, PHP 12.59, Python 48.73, Lua 60.55, so hxcpp is about 7.9x faster than HashLink and about 38x faster than Neko (derived from page data). September 2025 rerun (runtime seconds, cpp versus hl versus neko): Anonymous 0.1 / 0.19 / 2.68, BinaryTrees 0.05 / 0.32 / 1.42, Mandelbrot 0.13 / 1.32 / 8.83, NBodies 0.02 / 0.07 / 3.35, IntArray 0.01 / 0.03 / 3.07, Fib 0 / 0.04 / 0.58.
hardware: 2018 run: Intel Core i5-6600 @ 3.9 GHz, 15959 MB, Arch Linux x86_64, kernel 4.17.2. 2025 rerun: AMD Ryzen 7 7700 @ 5.39 GHz, 32 GB, Arch Linux, kernel 6.16.8.
stars_or_usage: 329 stars; the C++ target of the Haxe compiler (3,138 commits)
tradeoffs: hxcpp is the runtime support for the Haxe C++ backend: Haxe source is compiled to C++ and then built by the platform C++ compiler, so builds are slow (about 2 s per small program in the gist versus 0.1 to 0.2 s for neko, hl, js) and need a C++ toolchain; it ships its own garbage collector and runtime library and has the cppia scripting host. Output is native code, so it is the fastest Haxe target on most of these rows but the language semantics follow Haxe, not C++.
caveats: The measurements are an individual's gist, not an official suite, and neither Haxe nor hxcpp versions, the C++ compiler or its flags are given, so the run is below tier A (the benchmark code is public in HaxeFoundation/hashlink other/benchs). The 2025 rerun lists no totals and flags hlc returning 0 for every benchmark and lua erroring on BinaryTrees. Even against HashLink the win is not on every row: HL/JIT beat cpp on Anonymous in 2018 (0.29 s versus 0.38 s). Against the other baselines the win is not clear: the gist's 2018 totals put C++ 0.72 s next to Java 0.81 and JavaScript 0.96, and in the 2025 rows JVM and Node are faster than cpp on several rows (Anonymous 0.03 and 0.02 versus 0.1, BinaryTrees 0.02 versus 0.05, Mandelbrot 0.07 versus 0.13; derived from page data), while many cells are rounded to 0.01 s so small ratios are unreliable. The official HaxeBenchmarks site benchs.haxe.org (Xeon E3-1270 v6, Haxe 4.3.7, many targets) and the HaxeBenchmarks/benchmark-runner repo exist but the site was blocked (EGRESS_BLOCKED) so its numbers were not read. The hxcpp LICENSE.txt is a one-condition BSD notice ('See individual source files for additional license information'), so bundled third-party code carries its own terms.

name: Wasmer (LLVM backend)
baseline: Wasmtime (Cranelift) and V8 (Node.js)
workload: Libsodium's built-in crypto benchmark suite (about 70 primitives such as AEAD, hashes, signatures, box) compiled once to WASI and run in each runtime, December 2022 edition, wasmer with its LLVM compiler backend.
claimed_speedup: Geometric mean of per-benchmark time ratios over the 69 benchmarks present in both CSVs (derived from page data): wasmer-llvm is 0.872x the time of wasmtime (about 1.15x faster; faster on 54 of 69 benchmarks) and 0.747x the time of node/V8 (about 1.34x faster; faster on 60 of 69). The same data show wasmer-cranelift at 1.02x the wasmtime time (no gain) and wasmer-singlepass at 3.12x (slower).
license: MIT (repository); BUSL-1.1 for the LLVM and Singlepass compiler crates from Wasmer 6.0
tradeoffs: The LLVM backend compiles far slower than Cranelift and needs a matching LLVM install (LLVM 22 now); for startup-sensitive use the Cranelift or Singlepass backends are the practical choices. Wasmer is a runtime with its own WASIX layer, not a drop-in for the Wasmtime embedding API.
caveats: Ratios are derived by this agent from the raw per-benchmark CSVs (wasmer-llvm.csv, wasmtime.csv, node.csv) in the archived benchmark repo, geometric mean over 69 shared rows; the repo carries no 2022-12 README, so CPU model, runtime versions and flags for that edition are not stated. Compile time is not part of the measured numbers (LLVM compile is far slower). The 2021-Q1 README by the same author ranked WAVM ahead of wasmer-llvm and the author's 2026 post (blocked here, snippet only) reports Wasmtime ahead of Wasmer overall, so the win is specific to the LLVM backend and to this crypto-heavy workload. LICENCE WARNING: the repo root is MIT, but lib/compiler-llvm/LICENSE (and the singlepass crate) is Business Source License 1.1 for Wasmer LLVM 6.0.0 or later, with production use allowed only for Wasmer sponsors (change date four years after publication, change licence MPL-2.0); the December 2022 numbers were measured on the older MIT-era LLVM backend. Wasmer is itself a named baseline; this entry is evidence that its LLVM backend beats Wasmtime's default and V8 on steady-state throughput.

name: AssemblyScript (TypeScript-like to Wasm compiler)
baseline: JavaScript on V8 (Node.js v18.7.0), same n-body source compiled with tsc
workload: n-body simulation from the Computer Language Benchmarks Game (5 bodies, f64) in AssemblyScript Wasm, the same source transpiled to JavaScript with tsc, and a Rust Wasm version, timed inside Node.
claimed_speedup: First-party AssemblyScript/examples n-body README: AssemblyScript WASM 1606 ms, JavaScript 11640 ms, Rust WASM 1611 ms, i.e. 7.2x faster than JavaScript (derived from page data: 11640/1606) and level with Rust Wasm. Independent micro-benchmarks (LeanyLabs/assemblyscript-benchmarks, i5-8250, AssemblyScript 0.18.x) are mixed: factorial 14,076,129 versus 6,483,418 ops/s for JavaScript (2.2x, derived), calcSinLookup equal (11,450 vs 11,417 ops/s), while JavaScript is faster on add (697,262,505 vs 125,765,014 ops/s), squareArray, importCallback and averageIfLess.
compiler_and_flags: asc from the 'latest' npm package (exact version not stated), asconfig target wasm: optimizeLevel 3, shrinkLevel 0, converge, noAssert, runtime stub; Node v18.7.0 run with --nowasm-bounds-checks --nowasm-stack-checks --noliftoff --expose-gc; Rust Wasm built with rustc 1.64.0-nightly

tradeoffs: Strictly typed TypeScript subset (no any, closures and many dynamic features unsupported or limited); compiles through Binaryen to Wasm with its own GC runtime (stub, minimal or incremental); calls across the JS and Wasm boundary are costly so only compute-heavy kernels win; code must be written in a numeric style (unchecked(), f64) to approach the quoted speed.
caveats: The compiler repository itself carries no benchmark numbers (README and tests contain none, tests/benchmarks does not exist) and the project's website could not be opened, so the AssemblyScript book was not checked. The only first-party number is one n-body example in the separate AssemblyScript/examples repo: single workload, unspecified CPU model, asc version 'latest', and Node started with Wasm bounds checks, stack checks and the Liftoff tier disabled, which favours the Wasm side. The README says 'npm test [steps=1000000]' while tests/index.js defaults to 20000000 steps, so the step count behind 1606 ms and 11640 ms is ambiguous, and the table does not say whether it is the cold or warmed-up series. An earlier measurement of the same sample (AssemblyScript issue 1326, June 2020, AssemblyScript 0.10.0, Node 14.4.0, Windows 10, 20,000,000 steps) had JavaScript at 3.0 s and AssemblyScript at 5.6 s, the opposite result. Independent micro-benchmarks show JavaScript winning four of six cases. A search snippet attributing a 1.1x to 7.2x speedup range to an Iowa State paper could not be opened (host blocked). Perry's benchmarks/README.md names AssemblyScript with json-as as a peer but its AssemblyScript rows are empty ('skipped this sweep'). The emscripten C++ baseline from the lead was not found for this project.

name: aWsm
baseline: Wasmer; WAVM; Lucet; Node.js with Emscripten; wasm3 on microcontrollers
workload: PolyBench/C slowdown over native C, on x86-64, aarch64 (Raspberry Pi) and Cortex-M4/M7, for an ahead-of-time Wasm-to-LLVM compiler with a small C runtime.
claimed_speedup: x86-64 average slowdown over native: Wasmer 149.8%, WAVM 28.1%, Node.js + Emscripten 84.0%, Lucet 92.8%, aWsm 13.4%. aarch64: aWsm 6.7%. Cortex-M7 40.2% and M4 24.9%, versus 'more than 10x' for the wasm3 interpreter on microcontrollers (links wasm3's Performance.md).
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler through LLVM, so compile latency; the runtime is under 5K lines of C and the compiler under 3.5K lines of Rust; output is ELF objects; seven selectable memory-bounds-check mechanisms. Not a fit where interpreters or JIT are required.
caveats: README states 'these numbers are from May 2020'; hardware, compiler versions and flags are not given in the README (EMSOFT 2020 paper and Sledge Middleware 2020 paper hold the details, but www2.seas.gwu.edu was blocked). Wasmtime is not in the x86-64 table (the table shows Wasmer, WAVM, Node.js+Emscripten, Lucet); Wasmer and Lucet versions are 2020-era. Rust compiler plus C runtime, so only the generated objects and runtime are callable from C++. Repo remains active (last commit 2026-07-13).

name: FAFO (parallel EVM transaction scheduler on revm)
baseline: state-of-the-art sharded execution (paper's cost baseline); no sequential revm or pevm comparison found
workload: bench-sendeth: replay of native ETH and ERC-20 transfer workloads (zero contention 'none', hot-account 'hotn', and replayed real-trace generators) over a 2^30-account QMDB database with Merkleization every block, using revm for execution on one many-core node; the README claims throughput scaling and a cost comparison.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Over 1 million Merkleized EVM-Compatible transactions per second while maintaining state verifiability'; 'Near-linear throughput scaling up to 96 cores and beyond on a single machine'; '91% cheaper than sharded execution'. Search-result text of the paper (arXiv 2507.10757): over 1.1 million native ETH transfers per second and over half a million ERC-20 transfers per second on a single node. No timing of sequential revm or pevm on the same workload is given in the repo.
compiler_and_flags: Rust toolchain pinned by rust-toolchain.toml; benchmark run with cargo run --release through bench-sendeth/run.sh; revm 20.0.0 and alloy 0.11.1 per workspace Cargo.toml.
hardware: Repo states none. Third-party article snippet (OAK Research, not opened): one AWS server with 96 vCPUs, 786 GiB DRAM and six NVMe SSDs in RAID0 (22.5 TB).
tradeoffs: A transaction scheduler and pipeline (ParaLyze address estimation, ParaFramer with ParaBloom Bloom filters to group non-conflicting transactions into frames, ParaScheduler precedence graphs) rather than a new EVM interpreter: it runs revm and QMDB underneath, so gains come from parallel scheduling of independent transfers and are bounded by contention. Needs a very large machine (the benchmark initialises a database with billions of accounts, and the README's Docker setup asks for at least 256 GB of virtual disk and 32 GB of memory). Synthetic transfer workloads; the repo is described as ongoing research.
caveats: Not a faster-than-baseline claim in the sense of the listed baselines: neither the README nor bench-sendeth compares against sequential revm or pevm on a common workload (the only comparison in the README is '91% cheaper than sharded execution', a cost figure against a non-named baseline, with the methodology in a paper that is blocked here: layerzero.network and arxiv.org returned EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the paper's numbers come from search-result text only). The workloads are plain ETH and ERC-20 transfers, which is far easier to parallelise than general contract code; the paper is 'Under submission' (not peer reviewed). The repo holds a single 'Initial commit' dated 2025-06-26, so there is no development history to check, and the 96-vCPU machine is only known from a third-party article snippet. pevm and revm are catalogued separately, and Block-STM style comparison, if any, is in the unopened paper.

name: HashLink (Haxe virtual machine, Neko successor)
baseline: NekoVM (Haxe code compiled to the Neko target; also Haxe's Lua and Python targets, not stock Lua or CPython)
workload: The repo's other/benchs suite (Haxe programs Anonymous, BinaryTrees, Fib, FloatArray, IntArray, Mandelbrot, NBodies) compiled to each Haxe target and run as a process, startup time subtracted, in a third-party run.

Same table: Haxe Lua target 60.55 s, Python target 48.73 s, PHP 12.59 s (hl about 10.7x, 8.6x and 2.2x faster, derived). 2025 rerun on AMD Ryzen 7 7700: Fib hl 0.04 vs neko 0.58 s, Mandelbrot 1.32 vs 8.83 s. Slower than the other targets in the same table: C++ 0.72 s, Java 0.81 s, JavaScript 0.96 s total.

HashLink loses to hxcpp, JVM and Node in the same table (Mandelbrot 4.28 s vs 0.10 s for JavaScript); the 2025 rerun reports 'hlc result 0 but expected' correctness failures for the C backend. A second repository (haddock7/hashlink_benchmark, i7-7500U, HashLink 1.11.0, OpenSimplex noise) has HashLink VM 16.76 s, HashLink/C 5.91 s, native C 3.88 s, i.e. HL VM 4.32x slower than native C. name: LFI (Lightweight Fault Isolation)
baseline: LLVM-based ahead-of-time WebAssembly compilers (not named in README; Wasmtime, Wasmer and wasm2c are the usual ones)
workload: Run-time overhead versus native code on the SPEC 2017 benchmark suite (compatible subset) for in-process software sandboxing of native Arm64 and x86-64 code, compared with the overhead WebAssembly sandboxing imposes.
claimed_speedup: LFI: 7% runtime overhead (Arm64) or 8% (x86-64) for full read and write isolation, 1.5% (Arm64) or 6% (x86-64) for writes only, versus 'LLVM-based ahead-of-time WebAssembly compilers, which incur upwards of 20% runtime overhead' (lfi-research branch README).
compiler_and_flags: LFI-patched LLVM toolchain (lfi-llvm-toolchain); flags not stated in README.
tradeoffs: Sandboxes native C/C++/assembly rather than Wasm bytecode: no stable binary format, no platform independence, Arm64 and x86-64 only (RISC-V experimental); needs an LFI compiler toolchain and a verifier; ~64K (Arm64) or ~3K (x86-64) sandboxes of up to 4 GiB per address space.
caveats: The Wasm comparison figure is a summary line in the README; the per-runtime numbers sit in the ASPLOS 2024 paper (Yedidia, Lightweight Fault Isolation), which was not opened (scs.stanford.edu and zyedidia.github.io blocked). The baseline is not named in the README, so the exact WebAssembly runtime is unconfirmed (confidence capped at 0.5). A search snippet quoting a different source gives Wasmtime about 150% and wasm2c about 197% of native run time; not verified here. Different execution model from a Wasm VM: it replaces Wasm rather than running it faster.
found_via: WebSearch: 'software fault isolation sandbox faster than WebAssembly wasm2c Wasmtime WAMR overhead paper LFI OR Segue github'

name: Life (perlin-network)
baseline: wasmi (paritytech/wasmi, 2019 version) and wagon (go-interpreter/wagon)
workload: Three programs compiled to WebAssembly: 128-bit Pollard rho factoring, Snappy compression and recursive Fibonacci, timed end to end.
claimed_speedup: Raw results gist, real time: Pollard rho Life JIT 1.672 s, interpreter 2.178 s, wagon 4.349 s, wasmi 4.852 s; Snappy compress Life JIT 1.072 s, interpreter 2.977 s, wagon 5.443 s, wasmi 7.017 s; recursive Fibonacci Life JIT 3.898 s, interpreter 3.071 s, wagon 6.204 s, wasmi 5.811 s. So roughly 1.5x to 6.5x faster than wasmi with the JIT/AOT engine and 1.9x to 2.4x with the plain interpreter, and 1.6x to 5.1x faster than wagon with the JIT (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Pure-Go interpreter (no cgo) plus an experimental AOT/JIT engine that needs native code generation; implements WebAssembly MVP only (66 of 72 spec tests passed at the time) and has no WASI or modern proposals.
caveats: Numbers date from 2019 against the then-current wasmi (a much slower pre-register-machine design) and wagon, so they do not carry to wasmi 1.x/2.x, wasm3 or Wasmtime. No hardware, flags or versions are stated; the README only shows a chart image and links the gist. The repo was last committed in December 2019.

name: TinyKVM (Varnish KVM sandbox; per-request numbers come from libriscv/kvmserver)
baseline: per-request sandboxing by process fork, a new V8 isolate or WebAssembly-embedded interpreters (the alternatives the benchmark page names); native Linux process as the speed reference. Wasmtime and WAMR are not compared on any page opened
workload: kvmserver (separate repo built on TinyKVM) runs unmodified Linux server executables with a TinyKVM VM reset after each request: Rust minimal HTTP server, Deno hello world and Deno React page rendering; 1000 warmup requests, load generator against native, kvmserver and kvmserver ephemeral.
claimed_speedup: Page claim: 'We are able to run this benchmark 1.5-2 orders of magnitude faster than existing solutions' (previous React experiments: 'runtimes in the 10s of milliseconds with WebAssembly' and 'reset times of several milliseconds' for process fork or a new V8 isolate), against 55 us sandbox reset and 80 us total per-request overhead out of 690 us on the React benchmark. Against native it is slower: React page 646 us native vs 695 us ephemeral kvmserver (threads=1); Rust minimal server 13 us native vs 28 us; Deno hello world 17 us vs 50 us.
compiler_and_flags: Deno 2.3.6 run with --v8-flags=--predictable and built with deno compile; Rust server build flags not stated; TinyKVM build flags not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (32) @ 5.881Ghz
stars_or_usage: 823 stars; used by Varnish (VMOD-TinyKVM) and libriscv/kvmserver
tradeoffs: Needs /dev/kvm and Linux KVM (x86-64, with an arm64 feature matrix in docs); runs ordinary Linux programs at near-native speed with execution timeouts, memory limits and fork of an initialised program into many pre-initialised VMs. Syscalls needing the host cost about 1 us each; nested virtualization adds about 200 us; reset time grows with dirty pages and open file descriptors. Dual licence: GPL-3.0 or a commercial licence from Varnish Software.
caveats: The varnish/tinykvm README and docs carry no benchmark, only the qualitative 'run it in TinyKVM at the same speed' claim, and tests/ has no benchmarks. The numbers above are from libriscv/kvmserver, a separate project from the same author, and measure kvmserver plus TinyKVM, not TinyKVM alone. The fork, V8 isolate and WebAssembly baseline figures are described as 'previous experiments' with no table, so the 1.5-2 orders of magnitude claim is not reproducible from the page. Per request it is slower than native. Search snippets (Hacker News comment and a Medium post, neither openable here, snippet only) mention 2.5 us snapshot restore 'on par with Wasmtime' and about 14 us end-to-end per request; they were not used as evidence.

hardware: AMD EPYC (Family 25, Model 1) 2 logical processors at 2.4 GHz, 2GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.1
tradeoffs: Typed bytecode VM for the Type-C language (C11, minimal dependencies); no JIT, scavenger-only GC capped at 1MB allocations, not production ready, not documented or fully tested per its own notes.
caveats: Mixed result: the README says Type-V 'beats node on some benchmarks (unpublished)' but the published charts show it ahead of node --jitless only on the array test (by about 7%) and slower on fib(40) and member access. The numbers appear only in PNG charts that were read visually, and the baseline is V8 with the JIT disabled, i.e. only the Ignition interpreter. Kept as a flagged weak entry.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/bytecode-interpreter?l=c; README performance section (assets/bench_*.png)

name: UWVM2 (u2 interpreter)
baseline: wasm3
workload: Wall time of 383 .wasm modules that both uwvm2's u2 interpreter and wasm3 could run, plus WASI algorithm kernels (ChaCha20, SHA512, BLAKE2s), on AArch64 Apple Silicon.
claimed_speedup: Wall-time ratio uwvm/wasm3 geomean 0.5957 over n=383 modules (u2 faster on average), median 0.7116; ChaCha20 398ms vs 515ms, SHA512 202ms vs 220ms, BLAKE2s 3094ms vs 3427ms (internal time).
hardware: AArch64 Apple M-series (exact chip not stated)
tradeoffs: Template-specialized opfuncs trade code size for speed (Mach-O __TEXT about 1.4 MB), so u2 is not a minimal wasm3-class interpreter. C++26 codebase. Tiered interpreter + JIT design; supports many platforms, WASI P1, and mmap or allocator-based linear memory.
caveats: First-party section 9.1 of the u2 interpreter README, labelled by the authors as 'not universal claims', from an AArch64/Apple Silicon workflow with no CPU model, compiler or flags stated. The 383-module corpus lives in /tmp/uwvm2test and is not published, and the cited analysis note test/uwvm2test/u2_vs_wasm3_asm_stitch_analysis.txt returned 404 on raw.githubusercontent.com. The README itself says memory-heavy and branch-heavy kernels can lose to wasm3. Not compared with wasmtime, wasmer or WAMR; wasm3 is the only baseline.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/wasm-runtime?l=c%2B%2B (only C++ repo listed), then raw README of runtime/compiler/uwvm_int

name: VMIR
baseline: LLVM lli (LLVM IR interpreter)
workload: test/misc/src/sha1test.c over 64MB of random data, run as LLVM bitcode in the VMIR interpreter versus lli.
claimed_speedup: Core i7 3.2GHz: VMIR 4.8s vs LLVM LLI 7m39s (about 96x, derived from page data); native 0.39s. README: interpretation is about 10x slower than native.
hardware: Core i7 3.2GHz (exact model not stated); ARMv7 BCM2709 (Raspberry Pi 2): VMIR 1m42s, VMIR JIT 17.5s, native 3.54s
tradeoffs: Standalone C library that executes both LLVM bitcode (.bc) and WebAssembly (.wasm); the built-in libc is incomplete, no vector types, no C++ STL support, and the JIT exists only for 32-bit ARM and does not cover all instruction classes.
caveats: Single README table, one workload (SHA-1), no compiler or flags and no lli build configuration stated, so the 96x gap likely reflects lli being a deliberately unoptimised interpreter (the README says as much). The result is capped at tier C for that reason. lli is not a WebAssembly runtime baseline; VMIR is not compared with wasm3, WAMR or wasmtime. Last commit 2018.
found_via: GitHub: appcypher/awesome-wasm-runtimes C list; opened andoma/vmir README

name: w2c2
baseline: Wasmtime
workload: README CoreMark 1.0 of w2c2-translated C against native; the Wasmtime comparison is a libsodium benchmark reported in a blocked blog post.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Coremark 1.0: ~7% slower than native'. Blog (search snippet only, not on benchmark_url): libsodium benchmark Wasmtime 124.76 s vs w2c2-translated and compiled 73.38 s; CoreMark w2c2 2-5% slower than Wastrel which is 2-5% slower than native, Wasmtime 30-40% slower than GCC.
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time Wasm to portable C translator (inspired by wabt wasm2c): output must be compiled per module; runs on many OSes and architectures including big-endian; WASI and threads support; no JIT.
caveats: No compiler, flags or CPU stated anywhere I could open; the Wasmtime numbers are from a search-result snippet of Frank Denis's 2023-12 post (00f.net blocked) so unverified. README gives no baseline runtime for the CoreMark figure.
found_via: WebSearch 'wasm2c w2c2 translate WebAssembly to C faster than wasmtime native speed benchmark'; github.com/turbolent/w2c2 README.

compiler_and_flags: Engine versions listed (wasmtime 45.0.1/46.0.1, wasmer 7.1.0/7.3.0, V8 15.1.42/15.2.20, wazero 1.12.0, wasm3, wasmi_cli 1.1.0, WAVM prerelease); Go toolchain and build flags not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D (pinned to CPU 7) and Apple M4 Max
name: Wago
baseline: Wasmtime, Wasmer, V8 and wazero
workload: A 63-module corpus (PolyBench, Embench, Sightglass, CoreMark, AssemblyScript, zlib, zstd, QOI and others): compile latency (fresh process, load plus validate plus code generation) and cold execute latency (fresh process, load, compile, instantiate and first export call) as geometric means of per-module medians of 3 runs after 1 warmup, on AMD64 and ARM64.
claimed_speedup: README: 'compile 5x quicker and execute 1.9x faster than wazero' (the README figures are not reproduced in the committed study). Committed bench/runtime-corpus-study.md geometric means on Ryzen 7 7800X3D: compile wall wago 6.42 ms vs wazero 7.83, wasmtime 9.77, V8 14.44, wasmer 14.80 ms; cold execute wago 7.34 ms vs wazero 8.11, wasmtime 7.56, V8 16.84, wasmer 10.88, wasm3 9.91, wasmi 12.34 ms. On Apple M4 Max: compile wago 4.43 ms vs wazero 5.32, wasmtime 7.12, V8 14.75, wasmer 8.91; cold execute wago 4.77 ms vs wazero 5.27, wasmtime 5.95, V8 15.59, wasmer 6.76. So about 1.2x to 3.3x faster compile and 1.03x (wasmtime, AMD64) to 3.3x (V8, ARM64) lower cold execute latency (derived from page data). From the committed JSON, wago's internal Go-side compile time is a geometric mean 0.32x of wazero's over 63 modules (derived).
tradeoffs: Pure-Go Wasm-to-native compiler (amd64 and arm64); beta, WASI and the Component Model are external plugins. Not a steady-state throughput claim.
caveats: Cold-start wall times include process start, so the large wins over V8 and WAVM partly reflect the CLI startup cost of those engines, and wasm3/wasmi/wazero/wazy use different adapters; the execute metric includes compile. Wago's cold execute is within noise of Wasmtime on AMD64 (7.34 vs 7.56 ms). Compute-heavy steady-state speed was not isolated. The README's 5x and 1.9x figures point at wago.sh (blocked) and do not match the committed study. First-party benchmark (harness, JSON and study are public, CPU named, Go version and flags not), so held at C. Version is 0.0.0 beta.
found_via: github.com/topics/wasi?o=desc&s=updated listed wago-org/wago; opened its README, bench/README.md, bench/runtime-corpus-study.md and bench/results/runtime-corpus-amd64.json

name: WAMR in Zig (cataggar/wamr)
baseline: wasmtime run (default Cranelift JIT)
workload: Cold start of a 36-byte no-op module (subprocess wall time, 20 samples after 3 warmups) comparing in-process JIT, AOT cold and warm modes against 'wasmtime run', plus CoreMark steady state.
claimed_speedup: Cold start median: in-process JIT (.fast preset) 1.430 ms vs wasmtime 6.964 ms (about 4.9x faster); AOT warm 1.182 ms; AOT cold 2.552 ms. CoreMark steady state: wasmtime 26,462.6 iter/s vs JIT .fast 12,002.8 and AOT 12,442.8, i.e. wasmtime about 2.1x faster.
compiler_and_flags: Zig build with -Djit=true -Doptimize=fast; scripts/bench_jit_coldstart.py; Zig version and wasmtime version not stated in the doc.
hardware: Azure VM, 8 vCPU, AMD EPYC 9V74 80-Core Processor, x86_64
tradeoffs: Zig port of bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime kept as a separate fork (not drop-in for C++ callers without the Zig toolchain); passes the spec suite (257 .wast files, 65,135 assertions) per README; CLI is AOT/JIT only. Steady-state throughput is about half of wasmtime.
caveats: Cold-start win is on a trivial 36-byte module where wasmtime's fixed per-invocation cost dominates; the doc itself says wasmtime is about 2.1x faster on CoreMark. Single host, versions of wasmtime and Zig not stated, Small fork maintained with AI assistance (commit attribution and search snippet). Process spawn time is included in the numbers.
found_via: WebSearch: 'WebAssembly runtime paper faster than wasmtime V8 WAMR open source implementation github'

name: WARP WebAssembly compiler (wasm-ecosystem/wasm-compiler)
baseline: V8 Liftoff and TurboFan (also SpiderMonkey Baseline and Ion)
workload: Single-pass Wasm compiler and runtime for embedded systems; README quadrant chart of normalised compilation speed and execution speed against browser engines, benchmark inputs from Schleifner/open-wasm-compiler-benchmark.
claimed_speedup: README quadrant chart (normalised, higher is better), compilation speed / execution speed: WARP 0.8316 / 0.8172; V8 Liftoff 0.747 / 0.4275; V8 TurboFan 0.0423 / 0.8505; SpiderMonkey Baseline 0.8136 / 0.3456; SpiderMonkey Ion 0.099 / 0.8163. README: 'Industry leading compilation speed and close to native execution speed'.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark guide builds vb_bench with clang/clang++ cmake Release, -DINTERRUPTION_REQUEST=0 -DEAGER_ALLOCATION=1; V8 x64.release and SpiderMonkey optimized builds (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasm-ecosystem/wasm-compiler/develop/scripts/benchmark/Readme.md)
tradeoffs: Targets embedded and safety-critical use (AUTOSAR C++14, MISRA C++, no recursion, TriCore support); Wasm MVP plus some 2.0 features, no imported globals, tables or memories, no non-trapping float-to-int conversions.
caveats: Chart values are normalised scores with no raw timings, CPU model or workload list on the README page; the compared engines are browser JITs, not Wasmtime or Wasmer. WARP essentially ties TurboFan and Ion on execution (0.8172 vs 0.8505 and 0.8163) while compiling far faster, and ties SpiderMonkey Baseline on compile speed.
found_via: WebSearch 'github wasm JIT compiler C++ fast startup single-pass baseline compiler benchmark compared to wasmtime winch liftoff'.

name: wasm2go
baseline: wazero (an equivalent wazero-driven build of the same wasm module)
workload: A roughly 13 MB SQL parser/analyzer wasm module with 22 SQL benchmark queries, run once via wasm2go-generated Go (amd64/arm64 assembly bodies from an SSA register allocator) and once via wazero.
claimed_speedup: One-time cold compile 4.67 s (wazero) vs 0.56 s (8.4x); select_constant 49.3 us vs 2.7 us (18x); rank_dense_rank 220 ms vs 8.4 ms (26x); lag_lead 229 ms vs 10.0 ms (23x); json_extract_pipeline 878 ms vs 10.8 ms (81x); but q1_lineitem_pricing_summary 64.2 ms (wazero) vs 68.2 ms (0.94x) and q3_shipping_priority 33.9 s vs 37.3 s (0.91x), i.e. within 10% slower on long scan-heavy queries.
compiler_and_flags: go test -bench=. -benchtime=200ms; Go version and wazero version not stated
hardware: macOS on Apple Silicon (model not stated)
stars_or_usage: 87 stars, 7 forks; pkg.go.dev lists github.com/goccy/wasm2go/transpile v0.5.15
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time translator, not a runtime: the wasm module is baked into Go source (plus amd64/arm64 assembly) so the module is fixed at build time rather than loaded at runtime; very large modules produce multi-file output; the pure-Go fallback applies on other architectures; output is Go, not callable from C++.
caveats: First-party table on an unpublished 13 MB module, so not reproducible from the repo; the CPU model, Go version and wazero version are missing; the win is call-boundary and compile overhead on short queries, while compute-heavy scans are about 6-9% slower than wazero; no comparison with Wasmtime, Wasmer, WAMR or V8; github.com/hanzoai/wasm2go carries a copy of the same README.
found_via: WebSearch: Go WebAssembly runtime 'faster than wazero'; then github.com/goccy/wasm2go README and pkg.go.dev search 'wasm2go'

name: watr
baseline: wabt (wat2wasm) and Binaryen (parseText plus emitBinary)
workload: Compiling test/example/brownian.wat to a Wasm binary 500 times in a loop, in-process (JavaScript builds of each compiler); a second table compares watr's optimizer to wasm-opt over the 21 modules in test/example.
claimed_speedup: README metrics: watr 3,123 op/s versus wabt 859 op/s (about 3.6x, derived from page data), Binaryen 473 op/s (about 6.6x), the WebAssembly spec wast.js 1,509 op/s and wat-compiler 355 op/s. Optimizer table: watr/optimize about 110 ms in-process for the batch versus wasm-opt -Oz 990 ms as a CLI run (about 9x, but includes process spawn), with total output 19,734 B against 19,852 B for -Oz and 22,302 B for -O3.
tradeoffs: Pure-JavaScript, zero-dependency WAT compiler (about 44 KB minified) that also polyfills, minifies and optimizes; no native core, so large modules are slower than Binaryen.
caveats: Benchmark code is public (test/bench.js, browser-run, single brownian.wat input, N=500) but the README gives no CPU, browser or Node version. wabt and Binaryen are measured as their JavaScript/Wasm builds, not as native CLIs; for a 5.5 MB module the README itself says Binaryen's native core is faster (0.44 s versus about 2.6 s optimize plus 0.19 s compile). The 110 ms versus 990 ms optimizer comparison pits an in-process call against a spawned CLI.
found_via: Followed jz's benchmark README (lab case 'watr'), then opened github.com/dy/watr, its readme.md, LICENSE and test/bench.js

name: Web49 (miniwasm interpreter)
baseline: wasm3 (the fastest WebAssembly interpreter incumbent; wasmtime, wasmer, WAMR and V8 are not in the published charts)
workload: Wall-clock time of C benchmarks compiled with emcc -O2 and run once each by wasm3 and by miniwasm: binary-trees 16, coremark 3000, fannkuch-redux 10, fib_i32 40, mandelbrot 2000 (plain and SIMD), nbody 2000000, and a trap-execution test.
claimed_speedup: Bar charts only, no numeric table. Values read off the chart images by eye (approximate): fib_i32 40 about 3.0 s (wasm3) vs 1.17 s (miniwasm), roughly 2.6x (derived from page data); binary-trees 16 about 3.0 s vs 1.95 s (1.5x); fannkuch-redux 10 about 1.63 s vs 1.15 s (1.4x); nbody about 1.95 s vs 1.57 s (1.25x); mandelbrot 2000 about 1.46 s vs 1.30 s (1.1x); mandelbrot-simd about 1.06 s vs 0.91 s (1.2x); coremark 3000 about 3.4 s vs 3.2 s (1.06x). Trap test is slower: about 0.0055 s (wasm3) vs 0.027 s (miniwasm), roughly 5x worse.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark wasm modules built with emcc -O2 (bench.py default, no extra emcc flags). Engine built with make CC=gcc ('gcc is fastest in my tests' per README); the exact optimisation flags of the miniwasm and wasm3 builds, and the wasm3 version, are not stated.
hardware: 2020 MacBook Air (Apple M1, 8 GiB RAM)
tradeoffs: Single-threaded interpreter; wasm text format about 95%, binary format about 100%, spec tests about 75% complete per README (v0.0.1 first release). Bundles a custom WASI implementation and a small wat2wasm/wasm2wat/wasm2wasm toolkit that is much smaller than WABT or Binaryen. Uses threaded-code dispatch and basic-block versioning from the author's MiniVM; the README says computed-goto style macros (NEXT, LABEL) would need rewriting for MSVC.
caveats: Numbers exist only as PNG bar charts, each benchmark was run once by default (bench.py runs=1; trap and nop use more), on one M1 laptop with no CPU frequency or noise control. Margins on coremark and mandelbrot are within what laptop run-to-run noise can produce; only fib_i32, binary-trees and fannkuch-redux show clear gaps. Startup/trap handling is about 5x slower than wasm3. bench.py also lists wasmer and wasmtime as extra engines, but the published charts show only wasm3 and miniwasm, so no claim against wasmtime, wasmer, WAMR or V8 is verified. The Hacker News thread was not readable here (HN blocked); the search snippet says the author found WABT's interpreter too slow and wasm3 faster but interpreter-only. Chart values are my visual readings, not page text.
found_via: Hacker News via WebSearch (site news.ycombinator.com): 'Show HN: I wrote a WebAssembly Interpreter and Toolkit in C' (item 34310395); snippet linked the project at github.com/fastvm. HN thread itself not opened (blocked).

compiler_and_flags: StarlingMonkey built with cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DUSE_WASM_OPT=OFF -DWEVAL=ON; runtime is wasmtime serve (version not stated).
name: weval
baseline: generic SpiderMonkey (StarlingMonkey) JavaScript interpreter running on Wasmtime
workload: Octane benchmarks (Richards in the quoted PR) on SpiderMonkey compiled to Wasm and then partially evaluated by weval, run under 'wasmtime serve', versus the same interpreter without weval.
claimed_speedup: README: '3-5x speedups over the generic interpreter'. StarlingMonkey PR #91 quotes Richards score 676 with weval AOT versus 189 for the plain interpreter (about 3.6x, derived from page data). The PLDI 2025 paper's abstract (seen only as a search snippet) reports 2.17x average on SpiderMonkey and 1.84x on PUC-Rio Lua.
stars_or_usage: 149 stars; used by StarlingMonkey and ComponentizeJS for AOT JavaScript on Wasm
tradeoffs: Needs the interpreter source to be annotated with weval's intrinsics (include/weval.h) and a Wizer snapshot step in the build; the output is Wasm, so it still runs on any Wasm engine, but compile time and module size grow.
caveats: The baseline is the project's own un-wevaled interpreter, not a rival runtime, so the speedup says nothing about Wasmtime or V8 relative speed. The README gives a range without methodology; the PR does not state hardware or the Wasmtime version. The peer-reviewed paper (cfallin.org PDF, ACM DL) was blocked from this environment, so the 2.17x/1.84x averages are from a search snippet only and tier is held at C.
found_via: 'Related work' section of the quickjs-aot README (links the cfallin.org weval blog post and the arXiv paper), then the weval README
WebSearch 'weval Wasm partial evaluator SpiderMonkey speedup' after reading the weval README; opened github.com/bytecodealliance/weval and StarlingMonkey PR #91

name: wisp
baseline: wasmtime Winch (baseline compiler); wasmer Singlepass; wasmtime Cranelift on fib
workload: Whole-process wall time (including startup and compilation) of seven programs (primes, fib, matmul, raytrace, compress, json, regex) compiled to wasm32-wasip1, plus compile-only time for a 1.36 MB regex.wasm; median of 5 runs.
claimed_speedup: Compile-only regex.wasm: wisp 16 ms vs wasmtime Winch 24 ms, wasmer Singlepass 32 ms, wasmtime Cranelift 72 ms, wasmer Cranelift 82 ms. End to end: fib 34 wisp 0.022 s vs wasmtime Cranelift 0.024, Winch 0.031, wasmer Singlepass 0.028; raytrace 0.054 s vs Winch 0.066; json 0.263 s vs Winch 0.325; regex 0.308 s vs Winch 0.341 s.
compiler_and_flags: Release builds; wasmtime 49.0.1 and wasmer 7.5.0 release binaries; bench/run.py method documented in README.
hardware: Apple M5, macOS 27
tradeoffs: Compact (about 12,600 lines of Rust) runtime with validator, register-style interpreter and a single-pass AArch64 baseline compiler (macOS AArch64 only, Linux paths untested); passes 27,416 spec assertions on both engines; explicit bounds checks and no cross-block register allocation.
caveats: README states plainly that it is 1.5-2.5x slower than wasmtime Cranelift end to end on six of seven programs, loses to Winch on primes, compress and matmul, and wasmtime/wasmer compile in parallel and write artefacts while wisp compiles single-threaded, so the compile-time comparison is not like for like. Own benchmarks only, 0 stars, 15 commits when viewed, very new. Rust and AArch64-only compiler, not callable from C++ without bindings.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Whose baseline compiler is it anyway Wizard single-pass compiler Liftoff Winch Wasmer compile speed results' surfaced useless-husband/wisp

name: Wizer
baseline: Wasmtime instantiating and initializing the same module without Wizer pre-initialization (the README does not name the engine; Wizer embeds Wasmtime)
workload: Time to instantiate and initialize two Wasm programs with and without Wizer snapshotting their initialized state: a regex program and a UAP (user-agent parser) program.
claimed_speedup: regex 248.85 us -> 183.99 us (1.35x faster); UAP 98.297 ms -> 16.385 ms (6.00x faster); README: 'between 1.35 to 6.00 times faster instantiation and initialization with Wizer, depending on the workload'.
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; crates.io wizer about 171k downloads, wasmtime-wizer about 144k
tradeoffs: It is a pre-initialization tool, not an engine: it runs a module's init function and writes the resulting memory and globals back as Data segments, so the module can grow (hurting network transfer) and not every program benefits; the init code must be deterministic and free of host state.
caveats: First-party numbers with no hardware, flags or engine version stated; the benches/ sources linked from the README (regex-bench, uap-bench) returned 404 on the archived repo because development moved to bytecodealliance/wasmtime crates/wizer (the 'wasmtime wizer' subcommand replaces the CLI), so the numbers could not be re-derived here; the comparison is with and without the technique on one engine, not against another runtime.
found_via: crates.io API search q='wasm pre-initialization' (wizer, wasmtime-wizer)

name: BEAM.com (Erlang/OTP + Elixir single Cosmopolitan binary)
baseline: beam-emu.com, the same repository's own interpreter-only build (BeamAsm JIT off); no comparison against stock Erlang/OTP is published
workload: tests/bench/bench.erl run with the JIT build (beam.com) and the interpreter build (beam-emu.com): fib(32), lists:sort/map/foldl on 1,000,000 numbers, 200,000 map and ETS inserts and lookups, 5 MB binary match, 200,000 messages, startup time; best of 3 runs.
claimed_speedup: JIT build against the repo's own interpreter build, CI Linux x86_64 (ms, interpreter -> JIT): fib 70 -> 30, lists 249 -> 116, binary 249 -> 133, maps 83 -> 68, ets 70 -> 64, messages 111 -> 117; Linux aarch64: fib 139 -> 12, lists 411 -> 104, binary 290 -> 91; startup is slower with the JIT (--version 142 -> 222 ms on Linux x86_64). Stored kernel/stdlib zip entries cut start of beam.com --version from 193-202 ms to 143-146 ms (local, own earlier variant). No number against stock Erlang/OTP.
hardware: CI runners (shared machines) and a local Linux x86_64 box with 4 CPUs; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Packaging of the unmodified Erlang/OTP 29 ERTS and Elixir 1.20 as one Actually Portable Executable (Cosmopolitan Libc, about 50 MB, also a zip with the OTP applications); runs on Linux, macOS, Windows, FreeBSD, NetBSD and OpenBSD on x86_64 and aarch64; includes OpenSSL, SQLite and WAMR. The JIT adds 2.8 MB and 40 to 90 ms of start time. A second runtime (ERTS compiled to WebAssembly) runs on Cloudflare Workers and Deno Deploy at 1.2 to 1.4 times the time of the native interpreter in Node.js (WORKERS.md, October 2026).
caveats: Nothing in the repo shows BEAM.com beating stock Erlang/OTP. The BeamAsm JIT it ships is the one stock OTP already has on x86_64 and aarch64, so the fib 2x to 12x gains are JIT against interpreter, not against the incumbent BEAM. Its own measurements are first-party, from shared CI machines with noise it states as about 10%, with no CPU model or compiler flags, and the gate tables carry only relative limits. The only quantity that is faster by design is the packaging (one portable file, stored kernel and stdlib start about 27% faster than its own all-compressed variant). Kept as tier D because no recognizable baseline is beaten.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/sntran/BEAM.com docs/BENCHMARKS.md (raw.githubusercontent.com), README.md, docs/WORKERS.md

name: EOS VM Optimized Compiler (eosvmoc in AntelopeIO/spring)
baseline: EOS VM JIT and EOS VM interpreter (also WABT and Binaryen per the docs claim; WAVM is the origin of the code)
workload: Execution of WebAssembly smart contracts in an Antelope node: an LLVM-based tier that compiles a contract in the background while the baseline runtime (EOS VM JIT) serves it, then switches to the optimized native code.
claimed_speedup: No numbers in spring. A search snippet of the EOS VM documentation (snippet only) says native code from the optimized compiler is 'often an order of magnitude faster' than the same code in WABT, Binaryen, the EOS VM interpreter and the EOS VM JIT.
stars_or_usage: 30 stars; runs the Antelope/EOS blockchain node (Spring, formerly Leap)
tradeoffs: x86_64 Linux only; needs LLVM; has compile_monitor, compile_trampoline and code_cache components and a tier-up design so the first calls run on the baseline runtime; a leap issue is titled 'Reduce EOS VM OC's memory slice count allowing for higher parallelization' (seen in search results only); code created in part from WAVM, and the eos-vm-oc files carry WAVM's BSD-3-Clause notice (spring's top-level LICENSE is MIT).
caveats: spring has no benchmark for the OC tier: the repo has no README or docs for eos-vm-oc (only an 'About WAVM' note), and the spring README has no performance numbers. The 'order of magnitude' claim comes from a search-result snippet of the EOS VM docs (eos.io page could not be opened, host unresolvable) with no workload, hardware or compiler. Tier D by the assignment rule; the eos-vm repo is catalogued separately. Last commit date is from the commits page of main (Nov 2025); the releases page shows v2.0.0-dev1.3 on 27 Aug (year not displayed), so work may continue on release branches.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/AntelopeIO/spring (repo page, runtimes/eos-vm-oc listing, LICENSE) and WebSearch 'EOS VM OC eosvmoc optimized compiler LLVM benchmark vs eos-vm jit interpreter speedup AntelopeIO'

name: Wizard Research Engine
baseline: interpreter tiers of other WebAssembly engines (unnamed in the README)
workload: Hand-written x86-64 in-place Wasm interpreter (no bytecode rewriting) versus Wizard's own simple interpreter and, per README, versus interpreter tiers in other engines.
claimed_speedup: README: fast x86-64-linux interpreter is 'nearly 40x faster than the simple interpreter, and as fast as interpreter tiers in other engines'. No numbers against a named external engine on the page.
stars_or_usage: 514 stars; subject of the OOPSLA 2022 paper 'A fast in-place interpreter for WebAssembly'
tradeoffs: Written in Virgil, not C++, and the fast interpreter is hand-written x86-64 assembly for Linux only; README says the design favors flexibility and readability for research over ultimate performance. Benefit of in-place interpretation is low memory use and no rewrite step. WASI support is a work in progress.
caveats: Tier D research entry: the README gives no external baseline numbers and the paper (arXiv 2205.01183, ACM, Tufts copy) was not readable because those hosts are blocked, so any comparison with wasm3 or WAMR is unverified here. In-place interpretation is not claimed to beat the fastest rewriting interpreters (wasm3) on raw speed; the paper's claim is parity with a custom internal format plus lower setup time and space, which could not be checked. doc/ holds only benchmark_analysis_ideas.txt, no results. name: zig-evm (cryptuon)
baseline: its own sequential execution mode (no measured comparison against revm, evmone or geth; the README table of other EVMs is qualitative)
workload: Parallel batch execution of largely independent transactions, 8 threads, 100 to 1000 transactions per batch, versus sequential execution of the same batch.
claimed_speedup: README: 'measured 5-6x throughput gain over sequential execution'; table 100 tx 96.8 ms sequential vs 18.9 ms parallel (5.1x), 500 tx 485 ms vs 82 ms (5.9x), 1000 tx 970 ms vs 162 ms (6.0x). docs/BENCHMARK.md also lists an 'estimated' throughput table: Zig EVM about 10,000 tx/s simple transfer, geth about 3,000, revm about 15,000, evmone about 12,000 (so below revm and evmone in its own estimate; about 3.3x above geth, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.13.0, -Doptimize=ReleaseFast (as stated in docs/BENCHMARK.md)
hardware: 'AMD Ryzen 9 / Intel Core i9 (8+ cores)', 32GB (generic, no actual CPU model)
tradeoffs: Embeddable EVM engine with a C ABI (Python, Rust, Node bindings); wave-based parallelism needs independent transactions: cross-transaction CALLs in a batch, CREATE address dependencies and block-level operations are restricted; contended workloads fall toward 1-2x; conformance with Ethereum tests, differential fuzzing and a security audit are listed as not done.
caveats: The headline 'measured' table appears to be hard-coded, not measured. src/benchmark_demo.zig (the 'demo' step) prints a table titled 'Benchmark Results (Real-world estimates)' from a literal array (batch 100: sequential_ms = 96.8, parallel_ms = 18.9, identical to the README row; batch 500: 485.1 and 87.4 against README 485 and 82); src/benchmark.zig (the 'bench-full' step) prints 'Parallel Execution Speedup Estimates: 2 threads ~1.8x, 4 threads ~3.5x, 8 threads ~5.5x' as literal strings after timing only dependency analysis in that section; src/quick_benchmark.zig times a work-stealing pool with dummy work and a fixed 10 ms sleep as the completion wait. No code path found that times real parallel against sequential EVM execution (not every source file was read). The cross-EVM throughput table in docs/BENCHMARK.md is labelled 'estimated' and the README says the comparison table is 'directional, not a benchmark'. Per-opcode figures such as ADD about 500,000 ops/s (about 2 microseconds per ADD) would be far below revm or evmone. Similar to the earlier hard-coded-baseline precedent (zokio): likely reject-grade evidence for the speedup claim. A separate Zig EVM, 0xjojoex/evm.zig (3 stars, Apache-2.0 or MIT, 174 commits), publishes measured-looking numbers against evmone-base and revm-int on Apple M1 Max, ReleaseFast, Osaka snapshot, 2026-08-13: arithmetic loop 0.104 ms vs 0.109 ms vs 0.501 ms, SSTORE loop 0.162 vs 0.854 vs 0.875 ms, ERC20 transfer 3.761 vs 6.247 vs 6.084 ms, Snailtracer 19.965 vs 59.804 vs 37.990 ms (evmz, evmone-base, revm-int); only its README was read, so it needs its own record. Parallel-vs-sequential on the same engine is not a comparison with a listed baseline in any case.

name: Apogee (Lua 5.5 VM in Go, formerly luart)

name: LuaBridge
baseline: luabind (Boost-based Lua binding library)
workload: ThePhD/lua-bindings-shootout: Google Benchmark micro-benchmarks of binding operations (table get/set, C function calls, optional access, userdata access, member calls) across many C++ Lua binding libraries; median CPU time per operation in ns.
claimed_speedup: Median cpu_time in ns, LuaBridge vs luabind: table_get 102.5 vs 224.6 (about 2.2x), table_global_string_get 112.3 vs 199.5 (1.8x), table_global_string_set 15.7 vs 110.9 (7.1x), optional_failure 22.5 vs 147.5 (6.6x), optional_half_failure 138.1 vs 353.0 (2.6x), optional_success 210.0 vs 360.6 (1.7x), c_function 2950.6 vs 3442.4 (1.17x); ratios derived from page data. LuaBridge is slower than luabind on member_function_call (21449.3 vs 15694.7), userdata_variable_access (24414.1 vs 15346.0) and table_chained_get (276.2 vs 251.1).
compiler_and_flags: Windows x64 release build of lua_bindings_shootout.exe against PUC-Rio Lua 5.3.4 with Google Benchmark; the repo's CMakeLists sets /std:c++latest for MSVC and no explicit optimization flags; a WebSearch snippet says Visual Studio 2017 (snippet only).
hardware: 8 logical CPUs at 2592 MHz per the result JSON (CPU model not named; a search snippet says Intel Core i7 2.8 GHz); run dated 2018-09-28.
tradeoffs: Header-only, dependency-free binding layer for Lua 5.1+ and LuaJIT. No enumerated constants, no overloaded functions or constructors, at most 8 parameters unless TypeListValues is extended, no global variables outside a named scope (manual).
caveats: LuaBridge does not claim to be the fastest: its manual says it 'comes close to the highest possible performance' but 'is not quite the fastest' and that OOLua slightly outperforms it in some tests. In the same shootout it is slower than the raw Lua C API on every shared row (for example c_function 2950.6 vs 2131.0 ns, table_get 102.5 vs 17.6 ns) and slower than sol2 on most rows (table_get 102.5 vs 27.3), though it beats sol2 on optional_failure (22.5 vs 32.1) and table_global_string_set (15.7 vs 16.5). The win over luabind is mixed, as listed. Data is from 2018, and the shootout is run by the author of sol2, a competing binding library. Several benchmarks have no LuaBridge row (stateful_function_object, multi_return, table_set, table_chained_set). The maintained successor LuaBridge3 (kunitoki/luabridge3) is already in the catalog.
