baseline: QEMU user-mode (qemu-x86_64 and qemu-i386); Box64 is faster than FEX in the same tables
workload: 7-Zip benchmark (MIPS), dav1d (1 and 4 threads), glmark2 and OpenArena run as x86 and x86_64 binaries under QEMU user-mode, FEX and Box64 on an ARM Linux machine, by the Box86/Box64 author in March 2022.
claimed_speedup: x86_64 guest, FEX against QEMU: 7z 1486 vs 931 (1.6x, derived from page data); dav1d 1 thread 27.28 vs 11.24 (2.4x, derived from page data); dav1d 4 threads 52.67 vs 15.65 (3.4x, derived from page data); glmark2 164 vs 4; OpenArena 1.8 vs 0.083. x86 guest: 7z 1197 vs 691, dav1d 1 thread 21.75 vs 10.57. name: Hana Jit (LLVM-backed Python JIT, hanajit)
baseline: Numba 0.66 (and NumPy 2.x)
workload: Numeric kernels compiled through llvmlite: a 5-operation fused NumPy expression, float reductions, polynomial evaluation, dot product, fib(30) recursion and call/dispatch overhead, compared with NumPy and Numba.
claimed_speedup: 3.0x faster than NumPy and 3.7x faster than Numba on a 5-operation fused expression; fib(30) recursion 1.7x vs Numba; call/dispatch overhead about 46 ns (3.6x less than Numba). On plain scalar loops it is about equal to Numba (fp reduction 0.78 ms vs 0.74 ms, poly5 1.04 ms vs 0.96 ms, dot product 0.80 ms vs 0.74 ms); with the evolve() genetic tuner 0.23 ms, 0.22 ms and 0.31 ms against Numba 0.74 ms, 0.96 ms and 0.74 ms.
compiler_and_flags: LLVM via llvmlite; Numba 0.66 and NumPy 2.x as comparison; flags not stated
hardware: single core in a shared CI container (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Alpha Python package (about 3,000 lines) for numeric and array code; unsupported code falls back to the interpreter; also exports standalone x86-64 executables, WebAssembly and GPU kernels; Python-only, not callable from C++.
caveats: The README itself says ratios are the signal and absolute times are noisy (shared CI container, no CPU model); benchmark scripts exist in benchmarks/ (bench_experimental.py, bench_reductions.py, fourway.py) but were not run or read here. Plain scalar loops tie Numba because both use LLVM; the larger wins come from fusion, dispatch overhead and the opt-in evolve() tuner. The baseline is Numba, not PyPy; the README also claims 10-100x over CPython, which is not a named-incumbent comparison.
found_via: Package registries (vcpkg, conan, crates.io, pkg.go.dev, PyPI): PyPI simple index scan for names containing 'jit', then PyPI JSON descriptions read for benchmark claims (hanajit)

name: Higgs (higgsjs/Higgs JavaScript JIT)
baseline: V8 (its baseline compiler; its optimizing Crankshaft compiler is faster than Higgs)
workload: 26 JavaScript benchmarks run on Higgs, a basic-block-versioning JIT for x86-64, versus V8 compilers, as reported in the DLS 2015 paper 'Extending Basic Block Versioning with Typed Object Shapes' (arXiv 1507.02437).
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (paper not opened, arxiv.org is blocked): a WebSearch result summary says Higgs outperforms the V8 baseline compiler on all but one of 26 benchmarks, with speedups of up to 682%, but lags behind V8's Crankshaft, which performs 49% better on average. The Higgs README itself carries no benchmark numbers.
tradeoffs: Research JIT written in D (needs the DMD compiler), x86-64 and POSIX only, needs GNU make and GNU time. Not callable from C++ without embedding a D runtime.
caveats: Weak claim: it beats only V8's baseline (non-optimizing) compiler, and by the same summary loses to Crankshaft on average. The numbers come from a search-result summary of an arXiv paper that could not be opened here, so the paper's exact figures, hardware and V8 version are unverified; the paper itself is peer-reviewed (DLS 2015) and its artifact is this repo. Licence: no LICENSE file in the repo root and no GitHub licence badge, but source-file headers (e.g. source/main.d) state a Modified BSD licence with three clauses (opened). Last commit 2023-06-09 (a build/Python 3 pull request). Re-tier if a copy of the paper is reachable.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch restricted to news.ycombinator.com, query 'Show HN JavaScript engine written in C++ JIT faster than V8 benchmark' (HN thread 'LLVM based JavaScript JIT that beats V8 on Asm.js benchmarks' came with an arXiv 1507.02437 result naming Higgs); README, source header and commits page opened on github.com.

name: Instrew
baseline: QEMU and HQEMU (LLVM-based dynamic binary translation)
workload: LLVM-based dynamic binary translator running SPEC-style integer and floating-point benchmarks for x86-64 and RISC-V64 guests on x86-64 hosts, emulation overhead relative to native.
claimed_speedup: Search-result snippet of the VEE 2021 paper 'Efficient LLVM-Based Dynamic Binary Translation' (snippet only, PDF blocked): emulation overhead 53% for Instrew versus 648% for QEMU and 124% for HQEMU; RISC-V to x86-64 integer 76% (Instrew) vs 202% (QEMU), floating point 40% vs 1267% (QEMU). The README has no numbers.
tradeoffs: Needs LLVM at run time (client/server split in the repo); guests x86-64, AArch64, RISC-V64; hosts x86-64 and AArch64 (README).
caveats: Snippet only: numbers come from a search snippet of a peer-reviewed paper (VEE 2021) that could not be opened, so benchmark suite, CPU and flags are unverified; tier C here because nothing was opened, a verifier with the paper may raise it to B. The README cites VEE 2020 as primary paper; the snippet paper may be a later one. Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.
found_via: WebSearch 'dynamic binary translator OR dynarec faster than QEMU' returned the VEE 2021 PDF snippet; repo page and README opened on github.com / raw.githubusercontent.com

name: JPHP
baseline: PHP 5.6, PHP 7.0 and PHP 7.4 (Zend engine)
workload: Benchmark scripts run through './gradlew bench' on JPHP and 'php -f bench/src/bench.php' on PHP; the README states only the summary ratios.
claimed_speedup: README feature line: JIT (~2.5x faster PHP 5.6, ~1.1x faster PHP 7.0, ~13% slower than PHP 7.4).
tradeoffs: PHP 7.1+ language implementation on the JVM (PHP compiled to JVM bytecode and then JIT-compiled by the JVM), with Java interop, UTF-16 strings, threads and JavaFX/SWT GUI extensions. Not drop-in for PHP extensions.
caveats: Ratios only, no hardware or workload detail, and the README itself says it is slower than PHP 7.4 (the numbers predate PHP 8 and its JIT). Last commit 2020-07-07. Listed for completeness as a PHP-on-JVM claim, not as a win over PyPy, LuaJIT, V8 or HotSpot.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/jit?l=java topic page (jphp-group/jphp listed, 1.7k stars)

name: katsu
baseline: Node.js 26.8.1 (V8); Bun 1.4.0 and Deno 2.9.6 are also measured
workload: Cold start of a one-line console.log program (median of 25 runs after 3 discarded, hyperfine-style harness katsu-bench), plus peak RSS and binary size.
claimed_speedup: Cold start: katsu 0.0.5 1.55 ms vs Node 24.63 ms (the page says 15.9x faster), Bun 4.97 ms (3.2x), Deno 12.49 ms; peak RSS 2.44 MiB vs 48.14 MiB for Node; binary 1.7 MiB vs 139.0 MiB for Node. Compute is a loss: the katsu README gives fib(35) at 875 ms vs 53.4 ms on Node (16.4x slower, as of v0.1.6) and the katsu-bench README (https://github.com/tamnd/katsu-bench, also opened) shows fib 20-25x behind Bun.
compiler_and_flags: katsu built with cargo build --release, later runs from the published tarball; runtimes at latest releases of 2026-08-28; flags for the others not stated
hardware: Apple M4 (10 cores, 24 GB), macOS 15.8 (laptop, turbo on, frequency scaling on)
tradeoffs: Pre-alpha JavaScript/TypeScript runtime in Rust that plans a three-tier engine with a copy-and-patch baseline JIT. No module system, event loop, filesystem or standard library beyond console.log at the time of measurement. 12.31% of test262 passing at v0.1.8.
caveats: The author states the lead exists 'because it does less, not because it is better'. The measured binary is an interpreter with an inline cache, not yet a JIT, and compute is 16-25x slower than Node and Bun. Numbers are the project's own, from a laptop with turbo on and are labelled 'indicative' in the spec. Included mainly as a startup and footprint claim against V8-based Node.
found_via: WebSearch: github JavaScript engine JIT faster than V8 benchmark (katsu spec/15-benchmarks.md surfaced), then tamnd/katsu and tamnd/katsu-bench

name: libriscv
baseline: LuaJIT (JIT mode); README also compares against wasmtime, wasm3 and Luau
workload: Embedded scripting micro-benchmarks run in the sandbox as RISC-V guest code with binary translation, versus the same tasks as LuaJIT scripts: host-to-guest call overhead, syscall cost, integer math loops, sieve of 10M.
claimed_speedup: Binary-translated libriscv vs LuaJIT gist (median): call overhead 2 ns vs 156 ns, syscall (0 args) 10 ns vs 174 ns, integer math 6 ns vs 52 ns, sieve(10M) 80 ms vs 123 ms; fib(40) row shows parity (66 ns median both).
hardware: Gist does not state the CPU; the README names a Ryzen 7950X for its other charts (CoreMark 38223 vs 41382 native, about 92%).
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; same organisation maintains godot-sandbox (487 stars)
tradeoffs: Emulator and sandbox for precompiled RISC-V programs rather than a general JIT for a dynamic language; full binary translation needs a C compiler (GCC or TCC) at run time, or the generated C99 can be embedded ahead of time for platforms that forbid executable memory. Needs a RISC-V toolchain to build guest code.
caveats: Comparison is not like for like: guest code is C/C++ compiled to RISC-V, LuaJIT runs Lua scripts. The numbers come from author-run gists with no CPU or flags on the gist page, and the workloads are hand-picked for game scripting. README claims such as 'routinely faster than other interpreters, JIT-compilers and binary translators', '3 ns call latency' and 'can call the above function 5.25-7.25 times before wasmtime has called it once' are first-party; the fib(40) row is a tie.
found_via: GitHub topics page github.com/topics/jit?l=c%2B%2B (ranked 7th by stars), then the README and the LuaJIT comparison gist.
WebFetch github.com/libriscv/libriscv after considering bytecode VM sandboxes besides Wasm.
github.com/topics/jit?l=c%2B%2B listing (libriscv 'fastest RISC-V sandbox'); README and LuaJIT comparison gist opened

name: Luava
baseline: LuaJ 3.0.1 (the widely used Java Lua implementation); PUC Lua and LuaJIT are not benchmarked
workload: Ten Lua tasks (arithmetic loop, recursive fib, table insert/scan, string concat, closures, coroutines, hash table, OOP metatables, string patterns, sieve), paired interleaved runs against LuaJ, order-flipped, median, warm=6, iters=10, with -Dluava.jit.sync=true.
claimed_speedup: LuaJ time over Luava time: coroutines 234.7 ms vs 4549.9 ms (19.39x), recursive fib 243.8 ms vs 2538.6 ms (10.41x), arithmetic loop 33.7 ms vs 285.6 ms (8.47x), string concat 3.03x, table insert/scan 2.83x, hash table 2.68x, sieve 1.84x, string patterns 1.43x, closures 1.21x, OOP metatables 1.21x; all 10 tasks won.
compiler_and_flags: JDK 21+; -Dluava.jit.sync=true (synchronous JIT compilation); other JVM flags not stated
tradeoffs: Pure-Java Lua 5.4 (register bytecode VM with a tiered JIT, sandboxing with instruction limits, Java interop). Requires JDK 21+. MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft.
caveats: First-party numbers with no hardware stated. The baseline LuaJ interprets Lua 5.2 semantics, while Luava implements 5.4, so the tasks are not exactly equivalent. The README says what remains between Luava and PUC Lua (C) is dispatch cost, so it is probably still slower than C Lua and LuaJIT; neither is measured. Synchronous JIT mode is used for the benchmark, which removes background-compile effects. Very small project (52 commits, 2 stars).
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/jit?l=java topic page (luava listed)

name: mutable (WebAssembly/V8 query compiler)
baseline: HyPer (LLVM-based query compilation)
workload: TPC-H queries (per the EDBT 2023 paper abstract quoted in the README): queries are JIT-compiled to WebAssembly and executed by the embedded V8 engine, which tiers unoptimized to optimized code while the query runs.
claimed_speedup: 'We are able to match or even outperform state-of-the-art systems like HyPer' (README quote of the EDBT 2023 abstract; no numbers on the page).
stars_or_usage: 118 stars; academic system from Saarland University
tradeoffs: Research main-memory DBMS ('for research and fast prototyping'); AGPL-3.0 licence; relies on an embedded V8 build for code generation and execution; query compilation is one feature among many.
caveats: Snippet only: the numbers live in the EDBT 2023 paper (the README's PDF link at bigdata.uni-saarland.de is EGRESS_BLOCKED here), so the tier is capped at C even though the paper is peer reviewed (a verifier who can read it should consider B). Claim is 'match or even outperform', not a uniform win. Baseline HyPer is a closed-source binary. The repo ships a benchmark harness (benchmark/README.md, nightly dashboard at cb.mutable.uni-saarland.de, blocked here) but no result table.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'JIT compiling query expressions faster than LLVM JIT database engineering blog benchmark TPC-H compile latency' (query-compilation topic), then github.com/mutable-org/mutable README.

name: OpenResty luajit2
baseline: upstream LuaJIT 2.1
workload: Compile speed of the edgelang-fan compiler (a program whose Lua is generated by the fanlang compiler) after using the fork's JIT-compilable table.clone API.
claimed_speedup: 'We observe 7% over-all speedup in the edgelang-fan compiler's compiling speed whose Lua is generated by the fanlang compiler' (README note under table.clone; no hardware, version or method given).
stars_or_usage: 1.4k stars; maintained branch used by OpenResty
tradeoffs: Fork carries OpenResty-specific Lua/C APIs (table.clone, table.isempty, table.nkeys, thread.exdata, lua_setexdata), larger JIT limits (maxtrace=8000, maxrecord=16000, maxmcode=40960 KB) and a SSE4.2 CRC32 string hash that only applies when built with -msse4.2. Branch is v2.1-agentzh.
caveats: Only quantitative claim is a single anecdote, and it is credited to the new table.clone API (the application had to be changed to call it), not to a general LuaJIT speedup; baseline version, workload size and machine are unstated. The CRC32 string-hash and larger JIT limits carry no numbers. Lua-side usage rather than C++, but the fork is a drop-in LuaJIT C library embeddable from C++.
found_via: Blogs / talks: followed the LuaJIT-fork thread from WebSearch 'Lua JIT faster than LuaJIT benchmark blog new implementation'; opened the github.com README and raw README.md.

name: oxtra
baseline: QEMU 4.1.0 (x86-64 binary translation)
workload: Static x86-64 guest programs (a primes calculator and gzip 1.10.7 compressing floating-point CSV files of 132 kB, 526 kB and 13 MB) translated to RISC-V by oxtra and by QEMU; also instruction counts and memory use.
claimed_speedup: Paper text: oxtra is 'up to twice as fast as QEMU' for small inputs (primes below 10,000: oxtra median 20.68 ms vs QEMU 54.71 ms; 132 kB gzip), 'merely 25% faster' gzipping 526 kB and 20% faster with 13 MB; but for primes below 1 million oxtra is 35% slower than QEMU (3685 ms vs 2720 ms medians).
compiler_and_flags: Guests built with a modified musl-gcc fork (no SSE) and statically linked; host flags not stated
hardware: No real RISC-V hardware: everything ran inside system-mode QEMU running Fedora RISC-V (host CPU not stated); instruction counts given as a hardware-independent proxy
tradeoffs: Executes statically linked x86-64 programs only, no SSE support, needs a custom musl fork instead of glibc; RISC-V host only.
caveats: Student project paper (not peer reviewed, documentation/paper/Paper.pdf in the repo). Timings were taken under QEMU system emulation, which the authors say obscures the results. The README claims oxtra 'consistently beats qemu in our toy examples', but the paper shows a 35% loss on the larger primes workload. Benchmark input files ship with the paper source. Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.
found_via: WebSearch 'dynamic binary translator OR dynarec faster than QEMU benchmark' surfaced oxtra; then README and documentation/paper/Results.tex via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: pg_jitter
baseline: PostgreSQL LLVM JIT (llvmjit); also PostgreSQL's expression interpreter
workload: PostgreSQL 18.1 queries on 1M-row tables (aggregation, joins, wide rows, text, numeric, jsonb), JIT thresholds set to 0, median of 3 timed runs after 2 warmups, parallel workers off.
claimed_speedup: Benchmark page (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter/blob/master/bench/ARM64/0.3.0/BENCHMARKS_v18.md): SUM_int no JIT 44.859 ms, llvmjit 68.090 ms, sljit 42.401 ms, asmjit 42.201 ms, mir 45.620 ms; GroupBy_5agg no JIT 117.367 ms, llvmjit 149.033 ms, sljit 99.530 ms, asmjit 98.079 ms, mir 125.102 ms. README (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter): compile time 'tens to low hundreds of microseconds' (sljit) and 'hundreds of microseconds' (AsmJit) vs LLVM 'tens to hundreds of milliseconds'; average speedup over the interpreter TPC-C 8%, TPC-H 6%, ecommerce 14%, OLAP 42%, CRM ~400%.
compiler_and_flags: PostgreSQL 18.1; build flags for pg_jitter and PostgreSQL not stated on the page.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, 32 GB RAM, Darwin 25.2.0 arm64
tradeoffs: PostgreSQL extension only; beta quality by its own README; jit_above_cost must be lowered from 100000 to about 200-2000; avoid for point lookups; AsmJit backend only on arm64 and x86_64; adds embedded JIT libraries (sljit, AsmJit, MIR) in place of LLVM.
caveats: First-party benchmarks, one machine, ARM64 only (x86_64 results marked TBD); thresholds forced to 0 so LLVM compile cost is paid on every query, which favours the lightweight backends; per-query gains over the interpreter are small (README: sljit 5-25%); CRM benchmark is synthetic and built to show the strongest cases. The baseline is PostgreSQL's LLVM JIT, not one of the category baselines.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'asmjit benchmark code generation speed compared LLVM xbyak sljit JIT assembler performance' surfaced vladich/pg_jitter

name: PochiVM (copy-and-patch baseline compiler)
baseline: LLVM JIT at -O0 and higher optimisation levels (compile latency), and interpretation
workload: JIT code generation framework with a copy-and-patch baseline compiler (fastinterp); repo ships a TPC-H mini database backend (mini_db_backend, tpch_data) used to compare compile time and run time with LLVM.
claimed_speedup: From the Copy-and-Patch Compilation paper abstract as shown in a search snippet (snippet only): on TPC-H the compiler generates code two orders of magnitude faster than LLVM -O0 and three orders of magnitude faster than higher LLVM optimisation levels; generated code runs an order of magnitude faster than interpretation and 14% faster than LLVM -O0. The repo README only says the baseline compiler compiles in negligible time 'similar to interpreters' and generates 'better code than LLVM -O0'.
tradeoffs: Generated code is written through a C-like C++ API; research prototype, last touched 2021.
caveats: Snippet only: the paper (Xu and Kjolstad, OOPSLA 2021) could not be opened and the repo has no numbers; attribution of the TPC-H experiment to this repo is inferred from its tpch_data, mini_db_backend and fastinterp directories and the README's mention of copy-and-patch. The WebAssembly numbers in the same abstract belong to the WasmNow repo (already catalogued). Verifier with paper access could raise to B. Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.
found_via: github.com/topics/jit-compilation (WebFetch) listed sillycross/PochiVM; WebSearch 'copy-and-patch' gave the abstract snippet

name: PPy (Pretty Python compiler with LLVM JIT and AOT backends)
baseline: PyPy 3.11.15 (warm); also Numba 0.67, Codon 0.19.6, Cython 3.3, mypyc, Nuitka and CPython 3.14.5
workload: Collatz longest-chain search below 300000, kernel wall time, ten fresh processes each.
claimed_speedup: ppy run (LLVM JIT with Python integer semantics, overflow guards) 41.7 +/- 1.8 ms versus PyPy 3.11 52.8 +/- 0.5 ms (about 1.27x faster, derived from page data) and CPython 3.14 1068.8 +/- 5.5 ms; ppy build --unsafe 30.8 ms versus Numba 32.5 ms, gcc -O3 41.9 ms.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 13.3 -O3, clang 22.1 -O3 for the C rows; PPy built with ppy build / ppy run (LLVM); PyPy 3.11.15 and Numba 0.67 warm
tradeoffs: Compiles only the statically analysable subset of Python (guards fall back to CPython); LLVM backend needs the llvm extra; first ppy run pays about 640 ms to build into the cache (not in the table); the --unsafe rows drop overflow guards and use 64-bit wrap semantics. Python tool, not callable from C++ except through its C or C++17 source emission.
caveats: Single kernel; machine is described only as 'one machine' (no CPU model), and no PyPy reproduction script was seen in the repository, so the PyPy row is not independently reproducible. The eight-kernel suite in examples/15_algorithms compares against C, not PyPy. Pre-1.0 (0.6.0), 15 stars.
found_via: Package registries (vcpkg, conan, crates.io, pkg.go.dev, PyPI): WebSearch restricted to pypi.org 'JIT compiler Python package benchmark faster than PyPy and Numba' surfaced ppy-lang; PyPI JSON description read

name: R8 (NoClip, Rust V8)
baseline: Google V8 (TurboFan)
workload: 12 workloads from the js-engines-benchmark suite (arithmetic loops, recursion, object operations, memory, arrays, strings, cryptography, algorithms, WebSockets, databases, HTTP routing, package resolution).
claimed_speedup: js-engines-benchmark README (https://github.com/NoClip/js-engines-benchmark): R8 '3.08x faster overall' than Google V8 TurboFan across 12 benchmarks (suite total 19.43 ms vs 59.82 ms), individual speedups from 1.38x (arithmetic) to 11.13x (HTTP routing).
tradeoffs: Described as a pure-Rust engine 'based on Google V8 version 12.8'; no C++ API; extremely young (first visible commit 2026-09-14, about 20-27 commits).
caveats: Very low confidence. Same author runs the engine and the benchmark repo; hardware, date and flags are not stated; each workload takes only a few milliseconds; the benchmark repo has a commit about preserving upstream function names and verifying honest execution 'without R8 cheats', which suggests harness-gaming concerns; the r8 README table (arithmetic loops 4.13 ms vs V8 7.82 ms) does not match the 1.38x figure on the benchmark repo page. A from-scratch Rust reimplementation of V8 that beats V8 TurboFan 3x in a month is not credible without independent reproduction. Included so the verifier can check the harness; expect rejection if the benchmark is invalid.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'JavaScript engine faster than V8 benchmark github open source JIT Octane Speedometer results' surfaced NoClip/js-engines-benchmark

name: RapidUDF
baseline: native scalar C++ (GCC -O2 for the fib comparison; native loops for the vector cases)
workload: LLVM-JIT compiled expressions/UDFs: Fibonacci function, a trigonometric expression over a 4099-element double array, and a Wilson CTR formula over float vectors, JIT with SIMD vectorisation versus the equivalent native C++ function.
claimed_speedup: Vector expression 'acceleration ratio ... reaching 6.09' (207,713 ns scalar JIT / 207,145 ns native vs 33,962 ns vectorised JIT); Wilson CTR 'reaching 10.5' (69,961 ns native vs 6,661 ns vectorised JIT); scalar JIT fib at -O2 roughly on par with native (22,557 ns vs 19,246 ns), and faster than native -O0 (22,547 ns vs 38,933 ns).
compiler_and_flags: optimisation flag O2 for the vectorised tests (compiler for the native baseline not named); LLVM 18+ JIT
hardware: a CPU supporting AVX2 (model not stated)
tradeoffs: Requires LLVM 18+, highway, x86-simd-sort, sleef, abseil and others; C++17; supports a C-like DSL and table API.
caveats: The 6x and 10x wins are SIMD vectorisation (AVX2, SLEEF math) against scalar native code, not a JIT-versus-AOT effect; scalar JIT only matches native. No benchmark source for the quoted numbers was checked and the CPU model is unstated. Baseline is native C++, not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.
found_via: github.com/topics/llvm-jit (WebFetch) listed yinqiwen/rapidudf; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: regexr (Rust regex engine with x86-64/ARM64 JIT)
baseline: regex crate (Rust); PCRE2 with JIT as the second comparison
workload: Regex matching benchmarks (log parsing, URL extraction, Unicode letters, HTML tags, word boundary, email validation, alternation) reported as speedup relative to the regex crate.
claimed_speedup: regexr-jit 3.91-4.09x on log_parsing versus regex (pcre2-jit 3.57-3.71x), 1.95-1.99x on url_extraction (pcre2-jit 2.10-2.13x), 1.43-1.44x on unicode_letters (pcre2-jit 1.65-1.72x), 1.33-1.43x on html_tags (pcre2-jit 0.80-0.85x), 1.00-1.11x on email_validation, 0.88-1.01x on alternation.
tradeoffs: Adds lookarounds, backreferences and JIT without a C dependency; the non-JIT engine only matches regex crate speed; JIT is disabled on WASM; no C API mentioned; built for LLM tokenizer patterns.
caveats: README table only (a heatmap image carries the rest); hardware, compiler and flags are not stated and no benchmark source file was opened, so tier C. The JIT roughly ties PCRE2 JIT and loses to it on url_extraction and unicode_letters. The baselines are not in this category's baseline list (regex crate, PCRE2 JIT; pcre2 is catalogued separately).
found_via: Package registries (vcpkg, conan, crates.io, pkg.go.dev, PyPI): crates.io API search 'jit regex' and 'x86-64 jit' surfaced regexr; README Performance section read

name: rv32emu (tiered JIT)
baseline: QEMU v9.0.0 (RV32 user-mode emulation)
workload: RV32IM guest programs: nbench-derived numeric sort, string sort, bitfield, emfloat, assignment, idea, huffman plus dhrystone, primes and sha512, elapsed time averaged over 200 iterations, rv32emu with tiered JIT versus QEMU.
claimed_speedup: docs say rv32emu with tiered JIT 'outperforms QEMU v9.0.0 across all benchmarks'; the speedup is shown only as a normalised bar chart (docs/jit-bench.png) which reads by eye as about 1.25x (primes, sha512) to about 2.85x (assignment) of QEMU's speed (read from chart image, not stated in text). Reference table on the same page: Threadripper 2990WX Dhrystone 33,365 DMIPS (T2C) vs 2,533 (interpreter), about 13x (derived from page data); CoreMark 13,272 vs 1,835 iterations/s, about 7.2x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: RV32IM guest toolchain GCC v14.2.0; host build flags of rv32emu and QEMU not stated (DMIPS table lists GCC 14.2 on Threadripper and Clang 18.1 on Ampere eMAG)
hardware: Intel Core i7-11700 at 2.5 GHz, Ubuntu 22.04.1 LTS (QEMU comparison); AMD Threadripper 2990WX and Ampere eMAG (DMIPS/CoreMark table)
tradeoffs: RV32I[MAFC] guest only; an emulator rather than a general language JIT; tiered JIT (modes T1C and T2C in the page's tables); in system mode runs under Linux gain little because SFENCE.VMA flushes discard compiled blocks (page says so).
caveats: Numbers for the QEMU comparison exist only in a PNG chart, values here are eyeballed. The page text calls primes, sha512 and emfloat the biggest gains while the chart shows them among the smallest, so the prose and chart disagree. QEMU flags and the script that produced the chart are not named on the page (tests/interpreter_bench.py is for the libriscv comparison). Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot. A peer-reviewed VMIL'24 paper is referenced on the repo page but was not opened.
found_via: GitHub topics/jit?l=c (via WebFetch) led to RISC-V JIT emulators; then raw.githubusercontent.com docs/benchmark.md of sysprog21/rv32emu

name: rv8
baseline: QEMU (RISC-V user-mode emulation)
workload: RISC-V binaries translated to x86-64 by the rv-jit binary translator (hybrid interpretation and compilation of hot paths, macro-op fusion) versus QEMU.
claimed_speedup: Search-result snippet of the rv8 CARRV 2017 paper (snippet only, paper page blocked): performance 'on average approximately 75% faster than the leading competitor' (QEMU) and within about 30% of native x86-64 on some benchmarks. The README itself has no numbers.
tradeoffs: Targets RISC-V 1.9.1 privileged spec era binaries on x86-64 hosts only; only the Linux syscall proxy ABI is implemented for the JIT simulator (README).
caveats: Snippet only: the paper (rv8: a high performance RISC-V to x86 binary translator, CARRV 2017) could not be opened, so numbers, CPU, flags and QEMU version are unverified; a verifier with paper access could raise the tier (workshop paper). Repo last touched 2018. Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.
found_via: WebSearch 'dynamic binary translator OR dynarec faster than QEMU' and github.com/topics/binary-translation; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: sljit
baseline: PostgreSQL LLVM JIT (llvmjit) in the pg_jitter shootout
workload: Machine-code generation for PostgreSQL expression evaluation through the pg_jitter sljit backend (PostgreSQL 18.1, 1M-row tables, thresholds forced to 0).
claimed_speedup: pg_jitter README (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter): sljit compile 'tens to low hundreds of microseconds' vs LLVM 'tens to hundreds of milliseconds'; benchmark page (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter/blob/master/bench/ARM64/0.3.0/BENCHMARKS_v18.md): SUM_int llvmjit 68.090 ms vs sljit 42.401 ms, GroupBy_5agg llvmjit 149.033 ms vs sljit 99.530 ms; README calls sljit 'the most consistent: 5-25% faster than the interpreter across all workloads'.
compiler_and_flags: PostgreSQL 18.1; build flags not stated.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, 32 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Low-level stack-less JIT with a platform-independent API (x86, ARM, RISC-V, s390x, PowerPC, LoongArch, MIPS); you write the code generator yourself (no optimizer); used by PCRE2.
caveats: Indirect evidence: the numbers measure pg_jitter's sljit backend, not the library alone, and the sljit repo page has no benchmark of its own. Baseline is LLVM as used by PostgreSQL, not a listed baseline. Same first-party, ARM64-only caveats as pg_jitter.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'asmjit benchmark code generation speed compared LLVM xbyak sljit JIT assembler performance' surfaced pg_jitter, which names sljit as its fastest backend

name: stryke (strykelang): Perl 5 compatible interpreter with bytecode VM and Cranelift JIT
baseline: LuaJIT 2.1.1774896198 (also perl 5.42.2, Python 3.14.4, Ruby 4.0.2, Julia 1.12.6, Raku)
workload: Eight small scripts (startup, fib, loop, string, hash, array, regex, map_grep) timed end to end with hyperfine, mean of at least 10 runs with 3 warmups, process startup included.
claimed_speedup: Beats LuaJIT on 3 of 8: loop 0.74x, array 0.17x, regex 0.07x of LuaJIT time; near parity on string (1.21x) and fib (1.43x); loses on startup (2.20x), hash (3.40x) and map_grep (4.21x). Faster than perl 5.42.2 on all 8 (fib 27x, loop 29x) and than Python 3.14.4 on all 8 (loop 60x, regex 21x). The README ranks it second fastest dynamic language runtime behind LuaJIT.
compiler_and_flags: Cargo release profile opt-level 3, fat LTO, codegen-units 1, panic abort (from Cargo.toml); rustc version not stated
hardware: Apple M5, 18 cores
stars_or_usage: 5 stars; crate strykelang on crates.io (4454 downloads)
tradeoffs: Runs Perl 5 source (a superset with parallel primitives), so it is a Perl runtime rather than a Lua or general JIT; Rust crate, no C API seen; JIT can be switched off with STRYKE_NO_JIT=1.
caveats: First-party numbers read from the crates.io README (version 0.17.59); the harness bench/run_bench_all.sh is public but the compiler version is not stated, so tier C. Workloads finish in 2-14 ms and include process startup, so they mostly measure startup and tiny loops, not steady-state JIT speed. The regex row is not like-for-like (LuaJIT uses Lua patterns, stryke uses PCRE). LuaJIT wins 5 of 8 rows. The LuaJIT comparison is one column in a Perl-centred suite.
found_via: Package registries (vcpkg, conan, crates.io, pkg.go.dev, PyPI): crates.io API search 'faster than luajit' / 'baseline jit' surfaced strykelang; README Benchmarks section read from the crates.io README

name: WARP WebAssembly compiler and runtime (wasm-ecosystem/wasm-compiler)
baseline: V8 Liftoff and V8 TurboFan; SpiderMonkey Baseline and Ion
workload: Normalized compilation speed and execution speed of WebAssembly modules from the open-wasm-compiler-benchmark repo, WARP versus V8 and SpiderMonkey tiers and native clang code.
claimed_speedup: README quadrant chart (normalized scores, compilation / execution): WARP 0.8316 / 0.8172; V8 Liftoff 0.747 / 0.4275; V8 TurboFan 0.0423 / 0.8505; SpiderMonkey Baseline 0.8136 / 0.3456; SpiderMonkey Ion 0.099 / 0.8163; native clang 0.5 (comp. speed N/A) / 0.873.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark guide (scripts/benchmark/Readme.md, opened via raw.githubusercontent.com): clang/clang++, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, flags -DINTERRUPTION_REQUEST=0 -DEAGER_ALLOCATION=1; V8 built from source with gm.py x64.release; SpiderMonkey built with an optimized mozconfig. Versions not stated.
tradeoffs: Single-pass compiler and runtime aimed at embedded systems (x86_64, aarch64, tricore; aarch32 not implemented), written in C++14 with no external dependencies in production code; 187 kB stripped binary (AArch64, Clang 17, macOS). Compiles ahead of time into an ELF-like artifact that the runtime instantiates.
caveats: Result is a normalized unitless chart in the README; how scores are normalized and the CPU model are not stated, so the tier is C although scripts are public. WARP execution speed (0.8172) is slightly below V8 TurboFan (0.8505) and native clang (0.873); the win is the combination of compile speed and execution speed. The original research paper (Scheidl, 'Valent-Blocks', iCCECE 2020, doi 10.1109/iCCECE49321.2020.9231154) was not opened.
found_via: WebSearch: 'WebAssembly runtime JIT compiler faster than V8 Liftoff wasmtime paper open source github benchmark'; README and scripts/benchmark/Readme.md opened

name: WrenJIT
baseline: LuaJIT 2.1 (version and build flags not stated)
workload: Nine small paired kernels, each written once in Wren and once in Lua (sum, range for, fib, tak, ack, mutual recursion, deep recursion, binary trees, method call); the Wren timer includes JIT warmup and compilation, process startup excluded; best of five self-timed runs.
claimed_speedup: WrenJIT time versus LuaJIT time (lower is better): sum 0.641 ms vs 1.092 ms (0.59x), range for 0.074 ms vs 0.584 ms (0.13x), fib 39.4 ms vs 51.9 ms (0.76x), tak 2.224 ms vs 6.361 ms (0.35x), ack 0.024 ms vs 1.066 ms (0.02x), mutual recursion 0.098 ms vs 0.321 ms (0.31x), deep recursion 0.625 ms vs 6.724 ms (0.09x), binary trees 8.807 ms vs 19.8 ms (0.45x), method call 0.087 ms vs 0.448 ms (0.19x).
compiler_and_flags: CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release with a C99 compiler (compiler not named); SLJIT backend; pinned Wren 99d2f0b and sljit d9902b1; LuaJIT build and flags not stated
hardware: Apple M4 Pro
tradeoffs: Only runs Wren programs (a patched Wren VM, patches/0001-wren-jit-hooks.patch). One trace per loop PC, no side traces or trace chaining. Recursion is compiled by recognising complete bytecode shapes and emitting native kernels, not by a general method JIT. Tested on ARM64 and x86-64 only.
caveats: The README itself says these are 'narrow kernels, not a language-wide victory lap'. The recursive wins (ack 0.02x, tak, mutual recursion, deep recursion) come from shape-matched native kernels for those exact programs, so they say little about general Wren code. Sub-millisecond timings on several rows. The two programs are separate ports in two languages, so the comparison depends on how equivalent the Lua versions are. The LuaJIT version is not stated. The 'full report' page on a github.io host was not opened (host blocked in this environment). Single first-party author, 4 stars, repo started 2026-02-22.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/tracing-jit topic page (WrenJIT listed, 4 stars)

name: XS (xs-lang)
baseline: Node 20 (V8) and Python 3.13 (CPython), measured in the same README table
workload: Two programs run cold from disk: hello world (startup) and recursive fib(30); XS shown in --interp, --vm and --jit modes; best of three runs.
claimed_speedup: fib(30): XS --jit 31 ms vs Node 20 62 ms vs Python 3.13 71 ms (the --vm tier is 180 ms and --interp 950 ms); hello world startup: XS 3 ms vs Node 20 57 ms vs Python 3.13 15 ms.
hardware: Linux x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 (exact model not stated)
tradeoffs: A new language shipped as one static binary with compiler, language server, formatter and package manager; compiles to native code, JavaScript or WebAssembly. The JIT compiles only the opcodes in its supported set and falls back to the VM for the rest, and is meant for profiled hotspots.
caveats: The README says 'treat as indicative, not authoritative'. One compute benchmark, a call-bound recursive fib that favours a simple JIT, and CPU model and compiler flags missing. The Node version is old (20). A reproduction script (tests/bench_backends.sh, 'xs bench') is named but was not opened. Not a drop-in for JavaScript or Python programs.

name: LC Scheme BBV JIT (bsaleil/lc)
baseline: Gambit Scheme (gsc) and Chez Scheme; the repo harness compares against both but commits no results
workload: JIT compiler for Scheme on Linux x86-64 using lazy basic-block versioning with interprocedural code versioning; the README example runs fib(40) and prints the time, and tools/benchtimes/run.py plus tools/ecoop17-paper.sh reproduce the ECOOP'17 experiments over the classic Gambit benchmark set (ack, boyer, browse, compiler, conform, cpstak, deriv, earley, fft, fib, mbrot, nbody, nqueens, nucleic, peval, sum, tak, takl and others).
claimed_speedup: No numeric comparison against Gambit, Chez Scheme or any other baseline appears in the repo. README: 'time ./lc fib.scm' for fib(40) = 165580141, real 0.550 s, user 0.537 s, with no baseline. Search-result text of the ECOOP 2017 paper abstract says the technique removes almost all run-time type checks for several benchmarks, 'allowing the compiler to generate code up to 50% faster' (baseline not stated in the snippet; the paper itself was not opened).
stars_or_usage: 33 stars; three peer-reviewed papers (SFPW 2014, SFPW 2015, ECOOP 2017)
tradeoffs: Research JIT, Linux x86-64 only, written in Gambit Scheme and needs a modified Gambit (bsaleil/gambit) fork built first and gsc on PATH at build and run time; the build target is 'make debug'. Specialises by lazy basic-block versioning, so code size and entry-point table memory grow with version limits (the paper tracks code size and table sizes).
caveats: Tier D because no reachable source gives numbers against a named baseline. The ECOOP 2017 paper (drops.dagstuhl.de, EGRESS_BLOCKED), its artifact (DARTS 3.2.14) and the SFPW papers could not be opened, so the Gambit and Chez comparisons they probably contain are unread; this is a retier candidate if paper access appears. The repo carries the benchmark harness (tools/benchtimes/run.py defines Gambit, Chez Scheme, Pycket and several LC configurations, with hard-coded author paths and most systems commented out) and benchmark sources under tools/benchtimes/resultVMIL-lc-gsc-lc, but those directories hold preprocessed benchmark programs, not timing results. The fib(40) example is a demo with no comparison. Last commit 2019-05-11, so the project is abandoned.

name: Codon
baseline: CPython 3.10.7
workload: kostya/jit-benchmarks: single-threaded Benchmarks Game style programs run as the same Python source (CPython interpreter vs `codon build --release` native executable); time measured inside the program, so Codon compile time is excluded.
claimed_speedup: Best time (s), CPython vs Codon: binarytrees 73.15 vs 1.0; mandelbrot 37.52 vs 0.65; matmul 22.73 vs 0.25; nbody 53.72 vs 2.23; spectralnorm 20.69 vs 0.53; fasta 8.65 vs 1.66; fannkuchredux 4.04 vs 1.82; knucleotide 8.41 vs 2.69; brainfuck > 190 vs 2.05; brainfuck2 142.26 vs 1.91 (ratios derived from page data: about 73x, 58x, 91x, 24x, 39x, 5.2x, 2.2x, 3.1x, over 90x, 74x).
compiler_and_flags: Codon 0.15.5 built with `codon build --release -o <out> test.py` (tools/languages.rb); CPython 3.10.7 in Docker on Ubuntu 22.10.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 80 GB DDR4-3200
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler for a Python subset, not a drop-in CPython replacement: static typing, fixed-width ints, different semantics for some features; imports CPython modules through a bridge; native multithreading (no GIL), OpenMP and GPU support; compiler is written in C++ on LLVM.
caveats: Third-party suite dates from 2023-02-28 (round 1, Codon 0.15.5); pidigits, regexdna and revcomp did not compile or run under Codon (shown as '-'). It is a compiler, so compile times (4 to 7 s in the suite) are extra and speedups apply only to code in the supported subset. First-party README separately claims fib(40) 17.98 s on CPython vs 0.276 s on Codon and 'typical speedups ... 10-100x' (hardware not stated); not used for the tier. Compiler is C++ but the product is a standalone Python-language toolchain rather than a C++ library.

name: go-quickjs
baseline: QuickJS (C, release 2026-06-04) and goja (pure-Go JavaScript engine)
workload: Mozilla AreWeFastYet V8 version 7 suite (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes) as median of three fresh-process runs, plus QuickJS's own tests/microbench.js.
claimed_speedup: Versus goja (Apple M5 Max, Go 1.27.0): V8 v7 composite score 3,748 vs 720 (5.21x), wall time 22.51 s vs 53.37 s, 60.2% less allocation. Versus C QuickJS 2026-06-04 (AMD Ryzen 5 3600, Windows, Go 1.27.1): composite score 1,454 vs 1,315 (about 11% higher) and fixed-run total 1,690 ms vs 2,589 ms (0.65x QuickJS's time). Micro-benchmarks go the other way: 1.15x QuickJS's time by geometric mean over 71 tests.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27.0 (goja comparison, go-quickjs commit 04bbeec) and Go 1.27.1 (QuickJS comparison, go-quickjs 4629679 / v0.21.1); go build flags not stated; build flags of the C QuickJS binary not stated.
hardware: Apple M5 Max (macOS ARM64) for the goja comparison; AMD Ryzen 5 3600 (Windows) for the C QuickJS comparison.
tradeoffs: Pure Go reimplementation of QuickJS-NG with no cgo, WebAssembly or C toolchain, so it cross-compiles anywhere Go does; ships an embeddable engine, a qjs-style CLI and ECMAScript regex support. README reports 99,595 of 99,937 test262 variants passing (342 skipped). Go's switch dispatch costs about twice QuickJS per instruction, partly offset by running hot functions as trees of Go closures; Go GC instead of QuickJS reference counting; Intl through go-intl.
caveats: First-party numbers from a very young project (3 stars). The suite-level win over C QuickJS comes mostly from RegExp (0.30x of QuickJS's time) and Splay allocation setup; single operations are slower (slower on 48 of 71 micro-benchmarks, up to 3.5x on weak_map_set), and the author notes the fixed-run and scored-run margins disagree (0.65x time vs 11% score) because they time different things. The two comparisons ran on different machines and operating systems. Baseline goja is another pure-Go engine, not the category incumbent V8. LICENSE file carries Fabrice Bellard's copyright (derived from QuickJS-NG). Numbers were read from the repo docs; the discovering page was the go-js-engines-benchmark shootout (by the author of a competing engine, QJS) in a search snippet.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch '"faster than QuickJS" JavaScript engine interpreter blog post 2026 benchmark' returned the go-quickjs/go-js-engines-benchmark page (dated 2026-10-05); opened that repo, then the go-quickjs repo and docs/benchmarks.md.

name: goant (pure-Go JavaScript engine)
baseline: goja (pure-Go JavaScript engine); also compared with QuickJS (2021-03-27 build) and Node.js (V8)
workload: Octane 2.0 (chromium/octane pinned commit 570ad1cc), the eight workloads that ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark scores (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes), higher score is better, best of two runs, driven by goant-bench with each engine run as a command-line runner.
claimed_speedup: README Octane table, goant+JIT versus goja versus QuickJS: Richards 1374 / 218 / 836, DeltaBlue 929 / 271 / 818, Crypto 2320 / 127 / 1099, RayTrace 557 / 304 / 995, EarleyBoyer 822 / 540 / 1598, RegExp 276 / 212 / 268, Splay 2320 / 2138 / 3426, NavierStokes 6012 / 202 / 1971. Interpreter-only goant (JIT off): 227, 258, 257, 431, 536, 238, 1874, 467, so it beats goja on 5 of 8 (about 1.26x geometric mean, derived from page data) and beats QuickJS on none. goant+JIT beats goja on 8 of 8 (about 3.8x geometric mean, derived from page data; up to 29.8x on NavierStokes, derived from page data) and QuickJS on 5 of 8 (about 1.1x geometric mean, derived from page data). README: JIT is worth 3.1x over all fifteen Octane workloads. Node on the same machine scores 33,300 on Richards against goant+JIT 1374, so V8 is one to two orders of magnitude ahead. Third-party ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark README (ubuntu, 10/5/2026, goant v0.2.1): total score goant 981, goja 264, Paserati 401, QuickJS 1217, quickjs-ng 647, V8 48107, Node 40333.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26.3, CGO_ENABLED=0 go build; Octane at chromium/octane 570ad1cc; goja v0.0.0-20260723142020-b4aef50fa347 and otto v0.5.1 built through bench/gojarun and bench/ottorun runner modules; QuickJS 2021-03-27, duktape 2.7.0, Node 22.23.2, Deno 2.9.5, Bun 1.3.14.
hardware: Azure Standard_D8s_v5, Intel Xeon Platinum 8370C @ 2.80 GHz, 8 vCPU, 31 GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS x86_64, kernel 6.17
stars_or_usage: 7 stars; used in Robomotion automation robots (README)
tradeoffs: Pure Go, no cgo, single static binary of 11.1 MB, cross-compiles to every Go platform; ES2025 with modules, Temporal and Intl; 99.4% of test262 (53,247 of 53,573) versus goja 64.2%. The baseline JIT (amd64 and arm64) is off by default when embedded (WithJIT(true) to enable) and on by default in the goant command-line binary. Cold start 2.5 ms against QuickJS 0.8 ms and goja 2.0 ms; goja's own binary is 13.3 MB. Interpreter alone is 1.1x to 4.3x slower than QuickJS and 1.1x to 3.5x slower than ant, the C engine it was ported from. No tagged release yet, so go get must pin a commit; internal/engine is not a stable API. No optimizing JIT.
caveats: Project is first-party and young (7 stars, recent releases v0.2.0 and v0.2.1 in August 2026, no tagged release per its README), so the Octane numbers have not been independently reproduced; only the ahaoboy total scores are third-party. Only eight of fifteen Octane workloads are tabulated against the competitors (the same eight ahaoboy scores); the all-fifteen 3.1x JIT figure is from an earlier run on an identically specified instance, and the otto column was added later on the same machine. Best of two runs; Splay is noisy. QuickJS is the 2021-03-27 build, not the current release. goja wins Splay-like allocation-bound rows against goant interpreter-only, and QuickJS wins RayTrace, EarleyBoyer and Splay even against goant+JIT. In the third-party ahaoboy suite goant (981) scores below QuickJS 2026.06.04 (1217) while still beating goja (264) and Paserati (401); the ahaoboy README does not state the runner CPU. The JIT is a baseline compiler with differential fuzzing but no darwin/amd64 stress test.

baseline: Lua 5.4.7 (PUC-Rio reference interpreter, per the README environment table)
workload: kostya/benchmarks: Brainfuck interpreter (bench.b and mandel.b programs) and the primes test (Atkin sieve plus Trie prefix search), run as plain scripts under each interpreter.
claimed_speedup: bench.b: Lua/luajit 5.686 s vs Lua 37.051 s (about 6.5x, derived from page data). Primes: Lua/luajit 0.309 s vs Lua 1.056 s (about 3.4x, derived from page data). mandel.b: Lua/luajit 31.804 s (no plain-Lua row in the table).
compiler_and_flags: Interpreters run as `luajit file.lua` and `lua file.lua`; LuaJIT 2.1.1748495995 built with plain `make` from the openresty/luajit2 fork (docker/Dockerfile); README lists Lua 5.4.7 as the baseline.

stars_or_usage: 5.8k stars (repository description: mirror of the LuaJIT git repository)
tradeoffs: Lua 5.1-based, so Lua 5.3/5.4-only features (native integers and similar) are not available. JIT compilation is unavailable on some locked-down platforms. Memory use is higher on allocation-heavy tests (307.5 MB vs 145.2 MB for binarytrees in kostya/jit-benchmarks, 2023).

The README says the baseline is Lua 5.4.7 but docker/Dockerfile installs the Debian lua5.5 package (README and Dockerfile disagree, so the exact baseline version is uncertain). name: bc and dc (Gavin Howard)
baseline: GNU bc 1.07.1
workload: bc scripts run through tests/script.sh (add, subtract, multiply, divide), 1234567890^100000, a patched timeconst.bc script and two 100,000,000-iteration loop scripts; best of four runs, wall-clock seconds.
claimed_speedup: With -O2 and no LTO (wall time, GNU bc vs this bc): addition 2.54 s vs 0.88 s, multiplication 7.15 s vs 2.20 s, division 3.36 s vs 1.61 s, power 11.30 s vs 0.73 s, timeconst.bc 16.71 s vs 13.16 s. With -O3 -flto -march=native: power 11.08 s vs 0.71 s, multiplication 7.01 s vs 1.59 s. Slower on a plain for-loop script (16.60 s GNU vs 22.76 s this bc at -O2).
compiler_and_flags: clang 9.0.1; both bc builds compiled with the same flags: -O2 without LTO, then -O3 -flto -march=native, then -O3 -flto.
hardware: x86_64 machine running Gentoo Linux; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: POSIX bc plus dc in one binary and the bcl C library (callable from C++). Speed comes from packing several decimal digits per hardware integer and Karatsuba multiplication; author says the interpreter loop itself is slightly slower than GNU bc on scripts with little math.
caveats: Numbers are from bc 3.0.0 (2019) against GNU bc 1.07.1 with no CPU model, and the project has had many releases since; best-of-four runs; the win is arithmetic-library speed, not general interpreter throughput (loop scripts are slower or level); first-party measurements. GNU bc is not one of the category baselines and bc is a calculator language rather than a general scripting language.

baseline: gawk 5.1 (Linux) / 5.0.1 (macOS) and mawk 1.3.4, run with gawk -b
workload: AWK-style CSV and TSV processing on 5.2 GB HEPMASS all_train and 8.9 GB TREE_GRM_ESTN files: sum two columns, statistics, select, filter, group by key.
claimed_speedup: Sum two columns, macOS configuration, all_train TSV: gawk 10.4 s and mawk 10.8 s vs frawk (LLVM) 3.1 s and parallel frawk 1.7 s; TREE_GRM_ESTN TSV: gawk 14.0 s, mawk 42.0 s vs frawk 10.0 s / parallel 3.4 s. Linux configuration: gawk 23.1 s vs frawk 14.7 s on TREE_GRM_ESTN TSV. The doc says on a per-core basis frawk beats mawk and gawk but is slower than tsv-utils. Group By Key is a tie with gawk (14.8 s vs 14.8 s on macOS).
compiler_and_flags: frawk built with use_jemalloc and allow_avx2 features, LLVM and Cranelift backends 'with all optimizations enabled'; mawk on Linux compiled from source with -march=native; gawk invoked with -b; rustc/LLVM versions not stated
hardware: macOS: 16-inch MacBook Pro with 8-core i9 2.3 GHz (boost 4.8 GHz); Linux: dual-socket workstation with 2 x 8-core Xeon E5-2620v4 2.2 GHz, 64 GB RAM, Ubuntu 18.04
tradeoffs: AWK dialect with its own semantics (explicit numeric conversion needed in comparisons, CSV/TSV input modes), parallel mode splits input across workers; build needs LLVM or uses Cranelift; maintainer says bug-fix time is limited.
caveats: Author's own benchmarks, scripts are in info/scripts but compiler versions are missing and the numbers date from about 2021; frawk is slower than gawk or tied on some workloads (Group By Key) and slower than tsv-utils everywhere per-core; the doc itself asks readers to draw only modest conclusions. gawk and mawk are AWK implementations, not one of the listed category baselines.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/ezrosent/frawk while checking AWK and jq-style language interpreters; read info/performance.md

name: goja
baseline: otto (pure-Go JavaScript interpreter)
workload: Not stated in the README; general JavaScript execution ('on average').
claimed_speedup: README: 'it's 6-7 times faster than otto on average'; the Tengo README's fib(35) table independently shows goja 5,194 ms vs otto 48,539 ms (about 9.3x, derived from that page's data).
tradeoffs: ECMAScript 5.1 plus most of ES6+ in pure Go with no cgo; the README states plainly it is not a replacement for V8 or SpiderMonkey and that cgo-based engines are faster for computation-heavy code.
caveats: The README gives a ratio but no workload, hardware or method; an issue (goja#2) asked for the benchmark code and the maintainer's comment holds only the same sentence. Does not beat V8, QuickJS or any engine in the category baseline list. Baseline otto is itself slow.
found_via: GitHub javascript-engine topic page and WebFetch of github.com/dop251/goja README

name: GopherLua
baseline: CPython 3.4.3 (also C Lua 5.1.4, go-lua, otto, anko)
workload: Recursive fib(35) (result 9,227,465) timed once per implementation.
claimed_speedup: fib(35): GopherLua 5.40 s vs Python 3.4 5.84 s (about 1.08x faster, derived from page data), vs go-lua 8.13 s, otto 173.32 s, anko 182.73 s; but C Lua 5.1.4 is 1.71 s (about 3.2x faster than GopherLua). README: 'almost equivalent (or little bit better) performance as Python3 on micro benchmarks'.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.7; no flags stated; Lua 5.1.4 and Python 3.4.3
hardware: Windows 7 64-bit, 2 CPUs, 8 GB RAM (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Lua 5.1 VM in pure Go with a Go-friendly (non stack-based) API, goroutine and channel integration; README says it is 'not fast but not too slow'; using Go contexts for cancellation costs about 40% (7.5 s vs 5.3 s in the README example).
caveats: Very old single-benchmark wiki page (Go 1.7, Python 3.4, Windows 7) and the margin over CPython is about 8%; it is about 3x slower than reference C Lua. Included mainly as the baseline for Go-hosted Lua VMs and as a marginal result against CPython.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/yuin/gopher-lua README then the wiki Benchmarks page, after Wangshu and Tengo named it as their baseline

name: jrsonnet
baseline: google/jsonnet C++ reference implementation (v0.22.0-rc1); also go-jsonnet v0.22.0-rc1 and Sjsonnet 0.6.2
workload: Jsonnet evaluation wall time: real-world GraalVM CI and kube-prometheus manifests, the C++ jsonnet perf_tests and benchmarks suites, and Go jsonnet builtin benchmarks; mean and sigma tables per implementation.
claimed_speedup: C++ perf_test 'Large string join': jrsonnet 2.6 ms vs C++ 39.7 ms (15.44x) and Go 46.4 ms. C++ 'Tail call' benchmark: 865.2 us vs C++ 18,460.1 us (21.34x) and Go 2,559.0 us (2.96x). GraalVM CI: 34.4 ms vs Go 600.3 ms (17.47x), C++ did not finish within an hour. Kube-prometheus manifests: 43.6 ms vs Go 1,068.4 ms (24.52x), C++ took hours. Ratios as printed in the doc.
compiler_and_flags: Tested versions listed: jrsonnet 0.5.0-pre97, C++ and Go jsonnet v0.22.0-rc1, Sjsonnet 0.6.2, rsjsonnet 2026-03-23; Rust compiler, build profile and flags not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D 16-Core Processor, 32 threads
tradeoffs: Rust library and CLI; also ships libjsonnet.so-compatible C/C++ bindings plus Python (rjsonnet), WASM/JavaScript and in-progress Java bindings, so it is callable from C++. Adds experimental syntax extensions beyond standard Jsonnet (features guide). Jsonnet is a data templating language, so this only loosely fits the language-interpreter category.
caveats: Maintainer's own benchmark document: benchmark driver, run counts and build profile are not in the doc, only the source programs, versions and CPU. Many rows are microsecond to few-millisecond scale and probably dominated by process startup. C++ results are omitted for the heaviest workloads because they took hours, and C++ and Go are release-candidate versions. Repository was renamed from CertainLach/jrsonnet; deltarocks/jrsonnet is the canonical URL after redirect.
found_via: Blogs / talks: not named in any blog snippet; found by opening READMEs of niche language-interpreter implementations after the WebSearch snippets ran out. README states 'performance better than all existing implementations' and links docs/benchmarks.adoc.

name: KPHP
baseline: PHP 7.4 with OpCache (Zend micro_bench.php and bench.php); PHP 7.2 for the vk.com page timings
workload: php-src Zend/micro_bench.php and Zend/bench.php (after removing a couple of tests that do not compile), 5 runs each; plus vk.com page generation times and ML-style kernels measured by the authors.
claimed_speedup: micro_bench avg 3.297 s on PHP 7.4 vs 0.460 s on KPHP; bench avg 0.659 s vs 0.119 s ('KPHP is found to be 5-7 times faster'); vk.com/feed 10.1 s vs 0.95 s, vk.com/im 1.25 s vs 0.46 s, vk.com/ads 0.73 s vs 0.20 s (PHP 7.2); neural networks with huge matrices ~8 s vs 0.24 s; deep decision trees ~5 s vs 0.14 s; README: 'when your code fits best practices, it runs 3-10 times faster than PHP'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (PHP 7.4 with OpCache and without XDebug; KPHP compiler version and C++ flags not given).
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler from a limited, strictly typed PHP subset to C++ and then a native binary; no generators, anonymous classes, SPL or XML parsing, no call-by-name; existing PHP code usually needs rewriting to compile; the runtime is C++ and has a fast FFI.
caveats: First-party numbers with no CPU model or compiler flags. The doc itself marks the Zend micro benchmarks as 'absolutely synthetic' and warns it is wrong to say KPHP is always faster (code dominated by C-implemented PHP functions such as strpos or parse_url gains almost nothing). Baseline is PHP 7.4/7.2, far behind PHP 8 with its JIT, so today's gap is probably smaller. vk.com page timings and ML kernels are not reproducible from public code. The project website is on github.io (blocked here); the benchmark page was read from the docs/ directory of the repo.
found_via: Recalled PHP-to-C++ compilers while checking dynamic-language implementations; opened github.com/VKCOM/kphp, its raw README, docs/kphp-language/kphp-vs-php/benchmarks.md and the commit feed.

name: Lightstorm
baseline: mruby bytecode VM (inferred: the README chart labels the reference bar only 'Baseline', and Lightstorm compiles mruby bytecode)
workload: aobench ray-tracing benchmark (openbenchmarking aobench) compiled ahead of time to C through LLVM versus the interpreted baseline.
claimed_speedup: README: 'The compiled version (rightmost) decreases total execution time by nearly ~30%'. Reading the aobench.png bar chart: time about 78% of baseline for Compiled and about 71% for Compiled + escape + CSE; cache misses about 47% and 43% of baseline (values read off the chart).
compiler_and_flags: Generated C is built with -g -flto -O3 (LIGHTSTORM_CFLAGS in CMakeLists.txt); toolchain LLVM 19, CMake 3.28 or newer, ninja.
tradeoffs: Minimalistic ahead-of-time Ruby compiler (simplified Firestorm that targets C, built on mruby); it is not a full CRuby/MRI replacement and compiles only what the project supports.
caveats: One benchmark (aobench) and the numbers exist only in a PNG chart; the baseline is not named in the README (inferred mruby, not CRuby MRI or YJIT); no hardware, compiler version or run count; last commit December 2024.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/mruby page (DragonRuby/lightstorm, C++), then raw README and aobench.png

name: LLRT (Low Latency Runtime)
baseline: Node.js 20 (V8) on AWS Lambda
workload: AWS Lambda cold-start round-trip time (init duration plus function duration) of a DynamoDB Put function, ARM, 128MB; results shown as images in the README.
claimed_speedup: Up to over 10x faster startup and up to 2x overall lower cost compared to other JavaScript runtimes on AWS Lambda (README text).
hardware: AWS Lambda ARM, 128MB memory (no CPU model)
tradeoffs: No JIT, so peak compute is far slower than V8 and not recommended for compute-heavy work; partial Node.js API compatibility; ES2023 only; README marks it experimental and for evaluation purposes.
caveats: Only cold-start latency is measured, where QuickJS-based no-JIT startup wins by design; the headline is 'up to over 10x' with the measured numbers only in images; README methodology explains why round-trip time is used instead of Init Duration. Written in Rust, so it is a runtime to adopt, not a C++ library.
found_via: Direct fetch of awslabs/llrt following the WebSearch 'JavaScript interpreter engine C++ faster than QuickJS github benchmark results V8 jitless startup memory paper' (JS engines vs V8)
gist 'A list of JavaScript engines, runtimes, interpreters' (LLRT entry), then README header and 'Benchmark Methodology' section

name: LuaAOT (lua-aot-5.4)
baseline: Lua 5.4.3 interpreter (the stock interpreter the fork is based on)
workload: Numerical Lua benchmarks (the repository's experiments directory, e.g. binarytrees.lua) compiled ahead of time to C with the luaot compiler, versus the regular Lua interpreter.
claimed_speedup: 'For numerical benchmarks it can be twice as fast as regular Lua. But overall, it is not as fast as LuaJIT or Pallene.'
compiler_and_flags: Generated C compiled with gcc -shared -fPIC -O2 (README usage example); no benchmark flags stated.
tradeoffs: Modified Lua 5.4.3 with an extra luaot compiler that translates Lua bytecode to C (jumps become gotos, no bytecode dispatch); keeps full Lua 5.4 semantics and is embeddable from C/C++, but compiled modules must be built per script.
caveats: The README gives only a qualitative '2x on numerical benchmarks' figure with no table, hardware or timings; the paper that holds the experiments is referenced but not named or opened (scripts and programs are in the experiments directory). Based on Lua 5.4.3 (older than 5.4.7/5.5). Gains vary by program.
found_via: WebSearch 'Luau "Lua 5.4" faster interpreter benchmark numbers' -> hugomg/lua-aot-5.4; README and repo page opened
WebSearch: 'lightweight Lua interpreter faster than PUC Lua 5.4 github benchmark README "faster than" Lua 5.4 embeddable VM C++'

name: LuaAOT 5.4 (luaot)
baseline: Lua 5.4.3 reference interpreter
workload: Seven Benchmarks Game style Lua programs (binarytrees, fannkuch, fasta, knucleotide, mandelbrot, nbody, spectralnorm), 20 timed runs each; Lua bytecode compiled ahead of time to C and loaded as a .so module vs the stock interpreter.
claimed_speedup: README: 'For numerical benchmarks it can be twice as fast as regular Lua. But overall, it is not as fast as LuaJIT or Pallene.' Median wall time (s) from statistics/times-slow.txt, lua vs cor (the LuaAOT column per statistics/plot.r): binarytrees 3.51 vs 2.67; fannkuch 44.33 vs 21.9; fasta 5.04 vs 3.82; knucleotide 4.13 vs 3.44; mandelbrot 16.28 vs 6.16; nbody 17.76 vs 12.17; spectralnorm 39.83 vs 18.92 (ratios derived from page data: 1.31x, 2.02x, 1.32x, 1.20x, 2.64x, 1.46x, 2.11x).
compiler_and_flags: Generated C compiled with `gcc -shared -fPIC -O2 -g` (scripts/compile); Lua built with `make guess`; gcc version not stated.
tradeoffs: Modified Lua 5.4.3 with a Lua-bytecode-to-C compiler (luaot) that converts jumps to gotos and removes dispatch overhead; compiled modules need a C compiler and the modified Lua headers; one executable or .so per Lua module.
caveats: Hardware and CPU model are not stated in the files I opened (the README refers to a paper whose text I could not reach), so tier C although the raw timing data and scripts are public. Which column is LuaAOT was inferred from statistics/plot.r (impl_used lua, trm, cor, jit mapped to 'Lua', 'Trampoline', 'LuaAOT', 'LuaJIT'); the separate 'aot' column gives similar ratios (1.23x to 2.25x). Only seven benchmarks, mostly numeric; it is an AOT compiler rather than an interpreter, so it does not speed up code loaded at runtime. Upstream is Lua 5.4.3; GitHub fork status not checked.
found_via: WebSearch 'Lua 5.4 compatible interpreter faster than PUC Lua benchmark github C++ OR C' surfaced hugomg/lua-aot-5.4; opened the repo page, README, experiments and statistics directories, times-slow.txt, plot.r, scripts/compile and the commit feed.

name: LuaJIT Remake
baseline: PUC Lua 5.1 interpreter (also compared with LuaJIT's interpreter)
workload: The repository's luabench suite (a variety of Lua benchmarks, geometric mean over all benchmarks, each repeated 5 times), interpreter tier only with GC turned off for all implementations.
claimed_speedup: 'our interpreter is 34.6% faster than LuaJIT's interpreter, and 185% faster than the official PUC Lua5.1 interpreter'
compiler_and_flags: Built with `python3 ljr-build make release` inside docker (compiler and flags not stated in the README); the PUC Lua and LuaJIT comparison builds are not described.
hardware: Intel i7-12700H laptop, 32 GB DDR4
tradeoffs: Interpreter (and planned JIT tiers) are generated automatically from semantic bytecode descriptions; Lua 5.1 interpreter with a re-engineered runtime (tables use hidden classes). x86-64 Linux only.
caveats: Project is unfinished: garbage collection is not implemented (the README says GC was switched off for the competing implementations too), the package library and other standard-library functions are missing, and the multi-tier JIT is not complete, so the numbers are not production-comparable. Interpreter-only comparison, not against LuaJIT with JIT enabled. First-party numbers; the figure is an image and only the headline ratios appear in text. Last commit is 2025-02-18.
found_via: WebSearch 'Luau vs Lua 5.4 vs LuaJIT benchmark results github interpreter speed' -> sillycross.github.io 'Building the fastest Lua interpreter.. automatically!' (blocked); repo README opened

name: Mobius
baseline: Lua 5.4 and CPython 3
workload: Eight checksum-verified micro-benchmarks (integer arithmetic, fib(30), dense array ops, string-key table ops, string ops, nested loops, object create and destroy, mixed workload), median of five runs, in milliseconds.
claimed_speedup: README total 373.9 ms vs Lua 443.3 ms (0.84x of Lua's time) and CPython 1424.8 ms (0.26x, about 3.8x faster, derived from page data). Mobius is slower than Lua on fib(30) (1.23x), dense arrays (1.03x) and string-key tables (1.22x), and slower than CPython on string ops (1.69x), object create/destroy (1.14x) and the mixed workload (1.15x).
compiler_and_flags: buildy.yaml release configuration: C++17, -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -flto on Linux; which build produced the README table is not stated.
tradeoffs: Embeddable C/C++ scripting language with fibers, channels and worker threads, optional type locking, and a large built-in library (JSON, HTTP, SQLite, WebSockets). Version 0.1.0; no TLS yet. Integer division and modulo follow C semantics (truncating), unlike Lua and Python, per benchmarks/run_benchmarks.py.
caveats: The README table disagrees with the committed benchmarks/benchmark_summary_latest.json on the main branch (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bholcomb/mobius/main/benchmarks/benchmark_summary_latest.json): there Mobius totals 0.547 s vs Lua 0.420 s (Mobius about 1.3x slower than Lua, derived from page data) and CPython 1.419 s (Mobius about 2.6x faster). So the CPython win reproduces in the repo data but the Lua win does not. Hardware, Lua build and CPython version are not stated. Micro-benchmarks only; brand-new project with 3 stars.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'faster than Lua / faster than CPython bytecode virtual machine C++ benchmark' surfaced bholcomb/mobius; README Performance section and benchmarks/ directory opened

name: Monty (pydantic/monty)
baseline: CPython-based sandboxes: local Docker, WASI/wasmtime and Pyodide in Deno (per project docs); no CPython execution-speed claim in the repo docs
workload: Time to get a fresh sandbox and run `1 + 1`, and 10 REPL commands against an existing sandbox (project docs latency table).
claimed_speedup: OSS Monty new sandbox 0.80 ms (from a pre-created pool) vs 16 ms WASI/wasmtime, 195 ms local Docker, 2,700 ms Pyodide in Deno; 10-command agent run 0.40 ms vs 180 ms WASI, 700 ms Docker, 35 ms Pyodide; combined 1.20 ms vs 200 ms, 900 ms and 2,700 ms. README: under 1 ms from a running pool vs about 1,500 ms for a sandbox service.
tradeoffs: Minimal Python sandbox interpreter written in Rust for AI-generated code: no filesystem, environment or network unless functions and mounts are passed in; not a drop-in CPython replacement. Python, JavaScript and Rust packages; a commercial server variant (Full Monty) exists.
caveats: The claim is sandbox startup latency against container and Wasm sandboxes, not interpreter throughput against CPython, so it does not meet the category baselines. Footnote in the docs says Monty's number is a checkout from an already-created pool while the others start from nothing. No hardware stated. The repo has a monty-bench crate comparing Monty with CPython locally, but its numbers are not in the repo; a search snippet of project material said runtime speed is generally between 5x faster and 5x slower than CPython (snippet only). Vendor blog and docs site pydantic.dev blocked here.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Monty minimal Python interpreter Rust pydantic startup time vs CPython' (pydantic.dev article and Show HN thread titles); read the repo README, crates/monty-bench and docs/index.md.

name: newLISP Neo
baseline: CPython 3.14.4 and CPython 3.12.3 (also original newLISP 10.7.6 tree-walker, the project it derives from)
workload: Recursive fib(30), a 1-million-iteration loop (while and tail-recursive forms), and deep tail-recursion tests; wall time in ms for the newLISP Neo script versus the equivalent bench.py.
claimed_speedup: fib(30): newLISP Neo 42.6 ms vs CPython 3.14.4 86.0 ms (2.02x faster), CPython 3.12.3 186.9 ms, original newLISP 592.5 ms (13.9x faster than original); 1M-iteration while loop 31.3 ms vs CPython 3.14.4 37.2 ms (1.19x faster); tail-recursive 1M loop 17.3 ms (2.15x faster than CPython 3.14.4's while loop); 100M-step self-tail-recursion runs in 1,023 ms where CPython raises RecursionError.
compiler_and_flags: Build needs GCC/MinGW-w64 or Clang with computed-goto support; optimisation flags used for the timings are not stated
hardware: 'a Windows x86_64 host' (CPU not stated)
tradeoffs: Direct-threaded bytecode VM with automatic fallback to the classic tree-walking evaluator for dynamic-binding and metaprogramming code; generational GC with a 64 MB nursery; keeps the newLISP language (Lisp-like, not Python) and its GPL-3.0 licence; README says all 396 primitives pass the qa-dot suite.
caveats: First-party micro-benchmarks (fib, a counting loop, tail calls) on one unnamed Windows machine; the Python side is one hand-written bench.py per test; CPython 3.14.4 is the interpreter build without a JIT, and the tail-recursion rows compare against a CPython failure, not a time. Small young repository (earliest visible commit 2024-10-19). Forks irr/newlisp-spark and irr/newlisp-neo-fork (aarch64 support) exist and were not opened.
found_via: WebSearch (github.com/gitlab.com only): bytecode interpreter written in C++ "faster than CPython" OR "faster than Python" benchmark fibonacci README -> kimtg/newlisp-neo; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com and github.com

name: Nuitka
baseline: CPython 2.7 (Debian build) running pystone
workload: pystone, best of 100-1000 runs, uncompiled vs compiled with --lto=yes (and --pgo-c); script tests/benchmarks/pystone.py in the repo.
claimed_speedup: Debian Python 2.7 pystone 137497.87 uncompiled vs 460995.20 compiled with LTO (3.35x) and 503681.91 with PGO (3.66x); Nuitka-built Python 2.7: 144074.78 vs 479271.51 (3.49x) and 511247.44 (3.72x).
compiler_and_flags: nuitka --lto=yes --pgo-c (and --static-libpython=yes for the Python 3 variant); C compiler version for the table not stated (README says GCC 5.1+, Clang or MSVC 2022+ supported).

No CPU model. An independent timing in the Shed Skin README shows Nuitka 0.6.16 at 11.4 s on the sieve example, identical to CPython 3.11.0 (11.4 s) and only slightly faster than CPython 3.10.6 (13.4 s), so gains on other workloads can be near zero.

name: Paserati
baseline: goja (pure-Go JavaScript engine) and 'QJS' (QuickJS runner binary; README does not say whether it is native C QuickJS or the fastschema/qjs Wasm build)
workload: bench/bench.js (arithmetic and array microbenchmark) and bench/objects.js (object-heavy microbenchmark) timed with hyperfine via bench/hyperfine.sh.
claimed_speedup: bench/bench.js: Paserati 3.924 s vs goja 5.207 s (1.33x faster) vs QJS 4.945 s (1.26x faster); bench/objects.js: 6.169 s vs goja 7.015 s (1.14x) vs QJS 8.135 s (1.32x).

name: Porffor (AOT JavaScript/TypeScript to Wasm and C)
baseline: QuickJS and Node --jitless (V8 interpreter only); Node and Bun with JIT are NOT beaten
workload: V8 benchmark suite (v8-v7) composite score, higher is better; the suite is committed as bench/v8-v7.js.
claimed_speedup: Snippet of the porffor.dev site (page blocked, not opened): Porffor 6,646 vs Node without JIT 5,828, Bun without JIT 4,464, QuickJS 3,564; Node and Bun with JIT score 13 to 17x higher. Ratios (derived from the snippet): 1.14x Node jitless, 1.86x QuickJS.
tradeoffs: 100% AOT: compiles JS to C (with an IR) and also Wasm, with nothing interpreted or JIT-compiled; supports a subset of ECMA-262 (the README gives no conformance figure). Strong on startup, memory and binary size per the site, not on peak speed.
caveats: Snippet only: the numbers come from a WebSearch snippet that quotes porffor.dev; the site is blocked by egress policy so hardware, versions, flags and date could not be read, hence no benchmark_url and tier C at most. The committed repo README has no numbers (only 'compiled hello.js in 105ms, 33.7KB'). The README no longer says pre-alpha. Porffor is far slower than JIT-enabled V8 and JavaScriptCore on the same suite, so the win is over Node's interpreter-only mode and QuickJS. Third-party harness jlucaso1/js-compiled (also proggeramlug/js-compiled) benchmarks Porffor vs Node, Bun and scriptc on 22 programs, but its results are published only on GitHub Pages (blocked) and are not committed. The bench/ directory has 26 benchmark programs (richards.js, v8-v7.js and more) but no results file.

name: pqR (a pretty quick implementation of R)
baseline: GNU R (derived from R-2.15.0; the NEWS compares with R-3.4.0)
workload: Assorted R operations named in the release notes, for example paste and paste0 on character vectors and replacing parts of vectors or lists; the README states that the modifications substantially improve the speed of R.
claimed_speedup: NEWS: paste and paste0 are 'about two to six times faster than in R-3.4.0, and are usually faster than the stri_paste function from the stringi package'; replacing part of a vector or list with [ ], [[ ]] and $ is 'often faster', by up to a factor of two or more for scalar index and value.
tradeoffs: Source-compatible modification of R-2.15.0 (with some modules from R-2.15.1 and later), so it lags current R releases and package compatibility; adds some language extensions such as preliminary automatic differentiation. Includes the R packages and Fortran/C sources of the R distribution.
caveats: Claims are release-note statements without a benchmark script, hardware or compiler flags in the files read; the speedup baseline R-3.4.0 dates from 2017, not current GNU R. The project web page pqR-project.org was not opened. Last release 2020-07-23, so a modern GNU R (byte-compiled, 4.x) may have closed some gaps.
