name: prometeo
language: Python (transpiler that emits C calling BLASFEO)
baseline: CPython 3.7 (also compared with Nuitka and PyPy)
workload: Fibonacci benchmark CPU time for a Python-subset program transpiled to C; separate Riccati factorization benchmark against hand-written C with BLASFEO, NumPy and Julia (shown only as an image).
claimed_speedup: Fibonacci CPU time: CPython 3.7 11.787 s, Nuitka 10.039 s, PyPy 1.78 s, prometeo 0.657 s (about 17.9x faster than CPython, about 15.3x faster than Nuitka, derived from page data). Riccati factorization: comparable to hand-written C with BLASFEO, faster than NumPy and Julia (figure benchmarks/riccati_benchmark.png, no numbers in text).
hardware: Dell XPS-9360 with i7-7560U CPU at 2.30 GHz (README says 'all the benchmarks' ran on it)
tradeoffs: Not Python semantics: a statically typed DSL subset written in Python syntax with type hints, aimed at embedded high-performance linear algebra (BLASFEO). Output is plain C, so the generated code can be called from C++. Python-to-C transpile step needed; no dynamic features or standard Python libraries in the translated code.
caveats: The Fibonacci source and the compiler and flags used for the table are not in the repo (benchmarks/ holds only Riccati files), so the table is first-party and not reproducible from the repo: tier C. Python 3.7 and the Nuitka and PyPy versions are old and unstated. A statically typed integer recursion compiled to C beating CPython by about 18x is expected and says little about general Python code. Last commit 2022-05-19. Not an interpreter: the comparison is a Python-subset compiler versus CPython, filed here as the closest category.
found_via: Hacker News thread 'Show HN: Prometeo' (found via WebSearch 'Show HN Python implementation faster than CPython benchmark JIT subset'; the snippet quoted the Fibonacci numbers). Evidence judged from the repo README.

name: Pyccel
language: Python (transpiler that emits Fortran or C)
baseline: CPython (interpreted Python; version inferred 3.12 for the dev-branch table, tables also exist for 3.10, 3.11, 3.13 and 3.14)
workload: 13 numeric kernels (Ackermann, Bellman-Ford, Dijkstra, Euler, midpoint explicit/fixed, RK4, four finite-difference solvers, molecular dynamics, splines); execution time in ms, compilation excluded.
claimed_speedup: pyccel-benchmarks dev-branch execution-time table (ms, CPython column vs pyccel_gnu_c column; the Fortran backend is reported too): Ackermann 456.00 vs 1.33 (Fortran 1.28); Bellman Ford 1950.00 vs 3.28; Euler 3900.00 vs 6.94; Midpoint Fixed 40000.00 vs 47.40; RK4 19800.00 vs 57.00; FD Poisson 6140.00 vs 3.78; FD Laplace 729.00 vs 151.00; M-D 8530.00 vs 74.50; Splines 1770.00 vs 13.30. Ratios across the 13 kernels range from 4.8x (FD Laplace) to 1624.3x (FD Poisson), geometric mean about 336x for the GNU C backend (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: pyccel_gnu_c / pyccel_gnu_fortran configurations with -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -mavx -ffast-math (GNU compiler family, version not stated); Intel-compiler variants also reported
stars_or_usage: 398 stars; on PyPI (2.2.3 per the PyPI JSON API); JOSS 2023 paper (Pyccel: a Python-to-X transpiler for scientific high-performance computing) cited in the README
tradeoffs: Restricted, statically typed Python subset; emits readable C or Fortran that is compiled and wrapped as a Python extension; supports NumPy and SciPy calls through generated code.
caveats: Numbers come from the README of the Pyccel developers' benchmark repository (pyccel/pyccel-benchmarks), not from the project's own repo; CPU model, OS, GNU compiler version and Intel compiler version are not stated; the 'dev branch' table is dated 'Mon Aug 3 10:56:24 UTC 2026' and its Python version (3.12) is inferred from the result image file name devel_performance_312_execution.svg. Execution times exclude compilation (the README compile-time table, unit not labelled and presumably seconds, lists 0.33 to 8.31 per kernel across all tools). The CPython column is plain interpreted Python on scalar-loop style numeric kernels adapted from Burkardt and Barba examples (per the README; I did not open the kernel sources), so the large ratios do not transfer to code that already runs in NumPy. First-party benchmark (the Pyccel team's own repository), hence tier C even though the code, flags and Python versions are public. Pyccel is slower than Pythran on Dijkstra, M-D and FD Laplace in the same table. The JOSS paper was not opened (host blocked), so no peer-reviewed numbers are used.
found_via: WebSearch: pythran vs CPython speedup benchmark C++ Python compiler numba pyccel comparison (JOSS paper hit) -> github.com/pyccel/pyccel and pyccel-benchmarks; PyPI JSON API opened

name: Pyston
baseline: CPython 3.8
workload: Web-serving macrobenchmarks (Pyston's python-macrobenchmarks suite).

name: QJS (fastschema/qjs)

name: QuickJS (quickjs-ng)
baseline: Node.js (V8)
workload: Process start plus `console.log(1)` for each runtime, measured with the shell `time` builtin (txiki.js issue #301).

workload: Three public pyperformance benchmarks (richards, raytrace, unpack_sequence) run with S6's JIT enabled in CPython 3.7.

name: scriptc (Vercel Labs TypeScript to native compiler)
baseline: Node.js 24.18.0 (V8) and Bun 1.3.12; slower than both on sustained throughput per the same reports
workload: CLI process startup (median) of a compiled scriptc 0.0.16 executable against the same program on Bun and Node, plus idle memory of a node:http server.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: median CLI startup 1.78 ms for scriptc vs 21.29 ms for Bun 1.3.12 and 61.78 ms for Node 24.18.0 (about 12x and 35x, derived from the snippet); idle memory 1.9 MiB for a framework-free node:http server. Same coverage says Hono needs --dynamic and reaches 18.4k requests per second vs 70.5k for Bun.
tradeoffs: Compiles a typed subset of TypeScript/JavaScript and Node APIs to native code through LLVM, with no JS engine in static builds; --dynamic embeds quickjs-ng for npm dependencies and any-typed code and then loses the native speed. Runtime semantics differ from Node (see docs limitations page); experimental per the README.
caveats: Snippet only: the startup numbers come from WebSearch result snippets of news coverage (InfoQ and other outlets, all blocked here), whose original source and hardware I could not open; neither the scriptc README nor docs nor release notes contain a Node or Bun comparison. The repo has benchmarks/builds and scripts/bench-builds.mjs, which measure build latency and executable run time, not a Node or Bun comparison. Throughput is the weak side: GitHub issue titles (opened in the issue search page) say 'Bitwise operators lower to out-of-line scr_bit_* calls: 77x slower than Node on integer hot loops' (#357) and 'f64 loop indices prevent vectorization: byte loops still 2-6x slower than Node' (#113); later issues (e.g. #358) work on these, so figures may be stale. A search snippet also quotes one developer measuring about 7.5x slower than Node 24. Third-party harnesses (proggeramlug/js-compiled and jlucaso1/js-compiled) benchmark scriptc against Node, Bun and Porffor on 22 programs, but results are only on GitHub Pages (blocked) and not committed. Notable at 6k stars, so recorded despite thin evidence; tier C only because the snippets give numbers.

name: Shed Skin
language: Python (transpiler) generating C++; runtime library in C++
baseline: CPython 3.14 (headline claim); CPython 3.10.6 and 3.11.0 in the sieve timing
workload: Over 80 non-trivial example programs (more than 25,000 lines) in the examples directory, plus a sieve example with n=100000000 timed against several Python implementations.
claimed_speedup: Typical speedup of 1-100x over CPython 3.14 (average 20x, median 12x) across the examples. Sieve n=100000000: CPython 3.10.6 13.4 s, CPython 3.11.0 11.4 s, Shed Skin 0.9.9 1.9 s (--int32) and 1.8 s (--int32 --nowrap --nobounds), about 6-7x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Shed Skin flags --int32 --nowrap --nobounds for the fastest sieve run; C++ compiler and optimization flags for the 80-program measurement not stated on the page.
license: GPL-3.0 (compiler); MIT/Expat, BSD-3-Clause and BSL-1.0 for the C++ runtime library; examples individually licensed
tradeoffs: Accepts only a restricted, implicitly statically typed Python 3 subset: about 25 stdlib modules, no external libraries, no nested functions or variable argument counts; depends on the Boehm GC; programs often need refactoring; default integers are int64 (use --int32 for narrower).
caveats: First-party numbers with no CPU model or compiler version on the page; the 1-100x range includes programs chosen by the project and individual speedups are only in an image. The sieve table compares different tools at different CPython versions; README shows a separate comparison of Shed Skin and PyPy against CPython 3.10 (git tag performance_comparison) as an image only. Compared with Numba the README notes Numba defaults to int64, so int width affects the comparison.

name: Spinel
baseline: CRuby 4.0.4 (MRI interpreter) and CRuby 4.0.4 with --yjit
workload: 28 benchmarks in the repository's benchmark/ directory (mandelbrot, fib, matmul, nqueens, sieve, binary_trees, json_parse, ao_render and others), compiled ahead of time to native executables by Spinel versus the same scripts run by CRuby.
claimed_speedup: 'Geometric mean: ~8.5x faster than Ruby 4.0.4 with --yjit across the 28 benchmarks (~15.2x against the interpreter)'. Examples vs YJIT: mandelbrot 18 ms vs 938 ms (53.6x), matmul 6.1 ms vs 201 ms (32.9x), binary_trees 2.7 ms vs 13 ms (4.7x), json_parse 28 ms vs 133 ms (4.7x), csv_process 95 ms vs 396 ms (4.2x).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 13.3 builds the generated C; CRuby 4.0.4 (revision b89eb1bc) run with --disable-gems, and with --yjit for the JIT column; each cell is the mean of five runs under `perf stat -r 5`.
hardware: '32-core Linux box' (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: An ahead-of-time compiler for a Ruby subset (see the README Supported Ruby Features section), not a drop-in interpreter: it does whole-program type inference, emits C and invokes the system cc. Compiled binaries start in about 0.8 ms.
caveats: First-party numbers with only a core count for hardware. Sub-10 ms cells are dominated by process startup (README says the ratios are lower bounds). The README itself warns the fib row (44.6x vs YJIT) reflects the C compiler folding a pure call tree at build time. The README also notes YJIT is essentially identical to the interpreter on mandelbrot, nqueens, matmul, partial_sums and sieve.

caveats: Hedged, no-number claim kept as the single tier-D record of this run because the project is notable; the same FAQ tells users to write tight critical loops in C or C++, and no Janet-versus-CPython timings were opened, so the claim is unverified.

name: MiniVM
baseline: LuaJIT (HN title claim); the repo's test harness also runs plain Lua
workload: README shows fib(40) from test/fib/fib40.lua and a hello-world startup run; the HN title claimed performance on par with LuaJIT and C. test/bench.sh runs every test/*.lua file under minivm, luajit and lua and graphs the times, but no results are published.
claimed_speedup: No ratio in the repo. README: fib(40) 'took: 1725.805ms' and print hello world 'took: 0.307ms' with no baseline. HN title (2022): 'MiniVM: A zero-dependency cross-language runtime on par with LuaJIT and C'.
compiler_and_flags: README 'For Speed' build is make -Bj OPT='-O3 -flto' (not stated to be the build behind the two timings)
tradeoffs: Optimizing VM with a JIT built on Cuik's TB (git submodule); supports Linux x86-64, FreeBSD amd64, Windows x64 and WebAssembly only. Runs a Lua-like language, not full Lua compatibility. Written in C11 with minor GNU extensions, builds with GCC or Clang.
caveats: Tier D kept because the project is notable (1.7k stars) and the claim is named: the README gives only two raw timings with no baseline and says they 'aren't too representative yet'. The 'on par with LuaJIT' claim is from the title of a 2022 HN submission; the repo has since been rebuilt around a TB-based JIT, so the old claim may not describe the current code. A reproducible harness exists (test/bench.sh, lua.sh, luajit.sh, graph.py) but needs running by the verifier. A comment in the HN thread said it beats LuaJIT with the JIT off (snippet only, thread not opened).
found_via: Hacker News thread 'MiniVM: A zero-dependency cross-language runtime on par with LuaJIT and C' (found via WebSearch 'Show HN embeddable scripting language fast bytecode VM C benchmark Lua comparison'). Evidence judged from the repo.

name: TurboPython / tpy (typed Python to C++ without GC)
baseline: CPython (Shed Skin, Cython, mypyc, Nuitka and Codon appear in the README only as design contrasts, with no timings)
workload: None published: no benchmark against CPython, Shed Skin or Cython in the README, RELEASE_NOTES.md, TODO.md or the examples repo; the only timing script is scripts/perf/generator_frames.py, which compares generator forms inside tpy.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. The README says the output has no interpreter, no garbage collector, no reference counting and no GIL.
tradeoffs: Statically typed Python compiled through C++ (g++ 13+ or clang++ 19+) to a native binary; deterministic ownership model (Own[T], Rc, Arc[Mutex[T]]) instead of GC or reference counting; not a drop-in CPython replacement and no CPython packages (everything imported is TurboPython source, with a CPython extension-module export mode); Linux and macOS, WSL on Windows; standard library is a subset.
caveats: Early development, pre-1.0: the README says 'known bugs can produce wrong results silently' and BUGS.md lists many open items. No speed evidence at all, so tier D with very low notability (6 stars). TODO.md records one internal measurement (generator frames, gcc-14 and clang-20, default -O3, ms per 50 x 2M elements) that compares tpy generator forms with each other, not with CPython. Name collision: the PyPI package 'turbopython' is a different project (ribalba/TurboPython, version 0.1.0, March 2026) whose README claims 37.1x (Mandelbrot) and 59.4x (Fibonacci) over pure Python; those numbers do not belong to trozen/tpy-lang.

name: TypeScriptCompiler (ASDAlexander77, LLVM-based TypeScript AOT/JIT)
baseline: V8 (Node.js) running the same TypeScript/JavaScript; no named comparison found
workload: No speed benchmark found. The only measurements in the repo are peak working-set memory for a ray tracer (256x256 and 512x512) and an n-body simulation under the compiler's own three memory models (-mm=gc, -mm=rc, -mm=none), which compare the compiler with itself.
claimed_speedup: No speed numbers. README says the compiler produces native executables, WebAssembly or JIT runs 'no Node.js or JavaScript runtime required' and states no speedup against Node, V8 or Deno. Only memory figures in README and docs/memory-models.md: a ray tracer at 114 MB under -mm=none holds 4.1 MB with reference counting versus 5.8 MB with garbage collection.
tradeoffs: Compiles a TypeScript subset with its own semantics (strict null checks, a custom default library for JavaScript built-ins, no JS runtime) to LLVM/MLIR native executables, WebAssembly or JIT; garbage collection by default, with reference counting or no freeing selectable via -mm. Runs without Node.js, so Node APIs and npm packages are not available unless its default library provides them (not verified). Builds against LLVM/MLIR 22.1.8 (prebuilt MLIR releases exist).
caveats: Tier D: no numeric comparison against Node, V8, Deno or any named baseline found in README, docs/ (memory-models.md and others), tslang/ or scripts/ listings, or in a web search. The README header badge says the project is developed by Claude Code. Included at tier D only because the seed list names it and it has 776 stars; a speed claim vs Node would need an independent benchmark.
